title: MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

AI.tldr: MS-MLB is the first open benchmark for MS vs healthy control classification from whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048) with reproducible pipeline and external model submission pathway.
AI.motivation: While blood RNA expression data contains disease-associated immune signals, existing machine learning approaches for MS classification lack standardized, reproducible benchmarks with controlled data leakage and comparable evaluation metrics.
AI.method: Created MS-MLB benchmark using GSE17048 cohort converted to MS vs healthy control classification task. Implemented leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC/PR analysis, calibration measurement, and MS Research Score for evaluation.
AI.result: Gradient Boosting ranked best on holdout set: MS Research Score 93.83, AUC-ROC 0.989, sensitivity 0.950, specificity 0.778, F1 0.927, Brier score 0.050. Benchmark enables reproducible algorithm comparison with documented external submission pathway.
AI.conclusion: MS-MLB provides first standardized, reproducible benchmark for MS classification from blood RNA data, facilitating research comparison. However, it's for research only and not clinically validated. The framework is publicly accessible for community use and external model submissions.

title: When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters
summary: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

AI.tldr: CRAFTER: A method that keeps frozen pretrained forecasters unchanged but mines interpretable features from their prediction residuals to create lightweight post-hoc correctors, outperforming dedicated feature-engineering systems.
AI.motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to fix through fine-tuning. The paper aims to improve forecast accuracy without modifying the original model by analyzing its systematic errors.
AI.method: CRAFTER uses two complementary feature generators: 1) compositional search over raw input channels, and 2) LLM-generated named feature combinations, binary flags, and executable code. A validation-grounded gate accepts/rejects candidates, and a validation-selected corrector applies accepted features or leaves forecasts unchanged.
AI.result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER outperforms every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling improvement from correctors alone and reducing error of weakest backbones by up to 27%. Gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even on fine-tuned backbones.
AI.conclusion: CRAFTER provides an effective framework for corrective feature discovery that improves frozen forecasters without modification, while also serving as a benchmark for evaluating feature sources. The method demonstrates that modeling model-failure processes can yield significant forecast improvements.

title: PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs
summary: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a probabilistic programming language for LLM-based applications that quantifies and propagates uncertainty throughout workflows, enabling more reliable and trustworthy AI systems.
AI.motivation: Current LLM applications lack reliability due to uncertain outputs with no confidence measures. This uncertainty compounds in complex workflows involving multiple LLM calls and tools, making it hard for developers and users to trust the results.
AI.method: The paper proposes a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows that can quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout application workflows. It allows developers to experiment with different inference scaling techniques without modifying the core logic.
AI.result: The authors present an experimental study demonstrating the capability of their probabilistic language and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistic programming language approach addresses the reliability challenges in LLM-based applications by providing systematic uncertainty quantification and propagation, enabling more trustworthy AI systems.

title: Decoupling Perception from Description: Computation-Grounded Representation Alignment between Multivariate Time Series and Language
comment: 46 pages, 9 figures, including supplementary material. Submitted to AAAI 2027. Xinran Feng and Yi Xie contributed equally
summary: Training multimodal models to align time series with language runs into a self-supervision trap. The usual recipe asks an LLM to read a series and write a description, so label quality is capped by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. The data can never teach more than the labeler already knows. A second gap makes this worse: most datasets use a single variable, but the patterns that matter (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, co-occurring anomalies) appear only with several variables, right where the labeling LLM's limits are most exposed. These two problems create a trilemma: existing methods are reliable, realistic, or scalable, but none achieves all three. We resolve this by decoupling perception from description. Deterministic code computes a set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate series; the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. Perception, which LLMs do poorly, is handled by computation, while the LLM handles expression. This produces CGTime, our 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model. CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: it attains the best multivariate fact score on our held-out benchmark (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), a gap that survives Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. It also states verifiable numerical facts in generated captions more accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties.

AI.tldr: CGTime is a 4B-parameter time-series-language model that decouples perception from description using deterministic computation for pattern detection and LLM for verbalization, outperforming larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks.
AI.motivation: Current methods for training multimodal models to align time series with language suffer from a self-supervision trap where label quality is limited by the LLM's perceptual skills, especially problematic for multivariate patterns like cross-channel correlations and anomalies where LLMs perform poorly.
AI.method: The approach decouples perception from description: deterministic code computes statistics from real multivariate time series, while the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. This handles perception via computation and expression via LLM.
AI.result: CGTime achieves the best multivariate fact score (0.283 vs 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano) on held-out benchmarks, with statistically significant gaps that survive Holm-corrected tests. It also generates more accurate numerical facts and covers broader statistical properties.
AI.conclusion: By separating perception (handled by computation) from description (handled by LLM), the method overcomes the trilemma of reliability, realism, and scalability, producing superior performance on multivariate time series understanding compared to larger general-purpose models.

title: F$^2$Agent: Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence for Multimodal Trading
summary: With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, effectively leveraging multimodal data is becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading. Although recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have enabled the ingestion of multimodal inputs, existing methods fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise, due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. To address these challenges, we propose F$^2$Agent, a novel multimodal agentic paradigm driven by the Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence. F$^2$Agent first deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals. It further introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals. Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets demonstrate that F$^2$Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Notably, F$^2$Agent delivers returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics.

AI.tldr: F²Agent is a novel multimodal agent framework for financial trading that uses specialized agents to extract signals from diverse data sources, with adaptive fusion and noise-robust techniques to outperform existing methods by significant margins.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based trading agents fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and are vulnerable to market noise due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. With increasingly diverse information sources becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading, better multimodal approaches are needed.
AI.method: F²Agent deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals, then introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets show F²Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Specifically, it achieves returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA.
AI.conclusion: F²Agent demonstrates efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics by effectively leveraging multimodal data through specialized agent hierarchies and noise-resilient fusion mechanisms, significantly advancing the state-of-the-art in AI-driven financial trading.

title: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
summary: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

AI.tldr: Agentic Nesting is a multi-agent framework that encapsulates enterprise applications as AI agents in a nested hierarchy, enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous orchestration to solve data silos and process fragmentation.
AI.motivation: Enterprises face data silos and process fragmentation from multiple heterogeneous business systems. Conventional integration approaches (ESB, API gateways, RPA) suffer from high coupling, escalating costs, and limited intelligence.
AI.method: Proposes Agentic Nesting framework with three key components: 1) Encapsulating existing applications as autonomous AI agents (digital agent proxies), 2) Organizing agents in hierarchical stewardship topologies, 3) Using a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, with a unified conversational interface.
AI.result: Introduces two main contributions: 1) "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm, and 2) "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy. Explores generalization potential for heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data applications.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a novel approach to enterprise application integration by transforming legacy systems into intelligent agents within a nested hierarchy, enabling more intelligent, flexible, and maintainable enterprise orchestration compared to conventional methods.

title: Disentangling 3D Modeling from Spatial Reasoning
summary: In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm for spatial reasoning by explicitly disentangling 3D perception from reasoning, rather than jointly acquiring implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training. Our key observation is that modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, whereas large language models (LLMs) are particularly effective at compositional and symbolic reasoning. Motivated by these complementary strengths, we propose the Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR), a simple yet effective framework that reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using off-the-shelf expert perception models and fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. Without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies, DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks. Beyond its strong performance, DiSR offers improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency, demonstrating that explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence.

AI.tldr: DiSR disentangles 3D perception from reasoning using specialized perception models and fine-tuned LLMs, achieving competitive spatial reasoning without end-to-end training.
AI.motivation: Current approaches often jointly learn implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training, but modern perception models excel at 3D geometry while LLMs excel at compositional reasoning. The authors want to leverage these complementary strengths by separating perception from reasoning.
AI.method: Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR) uses off-the-shelf expert perception models to reconstruct physical world into structured 3D evidence, then fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence.
AI.result: DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies.
AI.conclusion: Explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence, offering improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency.

title: A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

AI.tldr: TIPEX is a framework that unifies two levels of parallelism in LLM-driven multi-agent systems - Replica Parallelism for exploring multiple solution paths and Structural Parallelism for concurrent execution within single paths - to improve inference efficiency while maintaining control over execution strategies.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems suffer from inefficient inference with multiple model invocations and complex coordination. Existing execution strategies directly impact system accuracy, latency, and computational cost, but different forms of parallelism lack systematic study and coordination.
AI.method: The paper proposes TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that models parallelism at two levels: Replica Parallelism (exploring multiple complete solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (concurrent execution within single paths through task decomposition). TIPEX unifies these parallelisms under a single execution semantics, allowing systematic combination and analysis of different strategies and parameter configurations.
AI.result: Experiments on GAIA benchmark show inference-time parallelism significantly improves accuracy and reduces end-to-end latency, though at increased token consumption cost. Replica and Structural Parallelism show complementary effects across task complexities, with intermediate-difficulty tasks benefiting most from coordination. Overly aggressive parallel strategies don't necessarily yield better performance.
AI.conclusion: TIPEX provides a unified framework for organizing and coordinating different parallelism levels in multi-agent systems. The complementary nature of Replica and Structural Parallelism suggests thoughtful coordination yields optimal results, especially for tasks of intermediate complexity, establishing a foundation for systematic inference-time parallel execution.

title: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
summary: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

AI.tldr: The Ignition Index is a validated metric that measures global workspace-like ignition transitions in transformer models, showing discriminative power across architectures and providing a quantitative bridge between neuroscience theory and AI interpretability.
AI.motivation: To create a validated quantitative metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models, bridging the gap between neuroscience theory and mechanistic interpretability in AI.
AI.method: Developed the Ignition Index (I) by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat that indicates abruptness of transitions.
AI.result: The metric shows 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure, identifies architectural differences (feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89%), reveals axis-specific ignition in recurrent models, detects training phase transitions, and disproves some scaling hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with significant measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized.

title: Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models
summary:
Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

AI.tldr: Matching only marginal distribution to Gaussian prior doesn't guarantee style-label independence in factorized generative models - style can still be highly predictive of class despite appearing Gaussian in aggregate.
AI.motivation: Current factorized generative models interpret matching style variable's marginal distribution to Gaussian prior as evidence of independence from class information, but this interpretation is incorrect and potentially misleading for evaluating style-class factorization.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing marginal matching places no constraints on class-conditional distributions, experimental demonstration with case-study model and four latent baselines across two datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10), plus investigation of mitigation strategies including conditional priors and empirical style banks.
AI.result: Models achieve near-zero global MMD (good marginal match to Gaussian) while linear probes recover labels with 74%-100% accuracy (vs 10% chance). Model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy but externally evaluated class-conditional generation only 16% success. Mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%-46% but don't fix within-class dependence. Conditional prior helps MNIST (0.97) but not CIFAR-10 (0.41), while empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: No divergence computed solely on marginal distribution of style latent can certify independence from class labels, and reporting marginal statistics alone doesn't verify the claimed factorization property in generative models. Additional constraints beyond marginal matching are needed.

title: Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis
summary: Orchestrated collectives of large language model (LLM) agents that debate and vote are an emerging form of computational intelligence: the intelligent behaviour resides in the \emph{interaction}, not in any single agent. They improve task accuracy, yet remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on the rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a decision. This paper develops a novel framework based on Koopman operator theory and validates its theoretical guarantees on multi-agent consensus dynamics. Treating the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph, we read its essential behaviour off the spectrum of its Koopman transfer operator, an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three machine-checkable certificates: the sub-dominant eigenvalue $λ_2$ fixes the intrinsic timescale of reasoning and yields a convergence deadline computable \emph{before} the debate runs; its eigenvector names the coherent factions the collective reasons in, and $|λ_2|$ certifies when that explanation is valid; and the leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log--log correlation $0.93$ and bounds it in 96\% of 24 configurations; attribution is exact whenever the spectrum certifies metastability; eight of 32 coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7\% fidelity; and a certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The study runs in minutes on a CPU, making spectral certification a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning.

AI.tldr: A Koopman operator theory framework provides spectral certificates for multi-agent LLM collective convergence, offering computable deadlines, faction identification, and compressed message auditing.
AI.motivation: LLM agent collectives that debate and vote exhibit intelligent behavior through interaction, but remain black boxes with no principled tests of convergence, bounds on debate rounds, or faithful accounts of decision drivers.
AI.method: Treats the collective as a nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph and uses Koopman operator theory to obtain an exact linear representation. Analyzes the spectrum of the Koopman transfer operator estimated from interaction traces to extract three certificates: convergence deadlines from sub-dominant eigenvalues, faction identification from eigenvectors, and compressed message bases from leading spectral coordinates.
AI.result: On an attention-consensus model, convergence deadlines tracked observed convergence with 0.93 log-log correlation and bounded it in 96% of configurations; attribution was exact when spectrum certified metastability; 8 of 32 coordinates preserved decisions at 99.7% fidelity; certificates learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates.
AI.conclusion: Spectral certification provides practical, machine-checkable certificates for trustworthy collective reasoning, running in minutes on CPU and offering convergence bounds, faction analysis, and compressed auditing capabilities for LLM agent collectives.

title: Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models
summary:
Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

AI.tldr: Woodpecker Distillation: A method that uses weak models to generate corrective patches for strong models' reasoning bugs, then distills this correction signal into the strong model to improve its mathematical reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite having the capability to solve them. These failures frequently arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than global incompetence, and these bugs are often repairable with corrective interventions.
AI.method: Woodpecker Distillation uses weak models to generate patches that correct reasoning bugs in strong models. It contrasts successful and unsuccessful patches at the same reasoning prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model through weak-to-strong training.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines where models are simply fine-tuned on weak patches or repaired trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The useful correction signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. Learning from contrastive local interventions through distillation is more effective than direct imitation for improving reasoning capabilities.

title: PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis
summary: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a data synthesis framework that creates multimodal rubric comprehension datasets to train models as rubric executors rather than question answerers, improving multi-rule, priority-aware instruction following.
AI.motivation: There's a gap between real-world multimodal instructions (which often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance) and current multimodal training data (which reduce instruction following to answering single self-contained questions). Most models lack the ability to properly handle complex, prioritized rubrics.
AI.method: Proposed PRISM, a four-stage data synthesis framework: 1) Generate persona-task pairs, 2) Create prefix-guided rule sets, 3) Produce quality-filtered rubrics, 4) Generate structured verification traces. Also introduced PRISM-Eval with Loose and Strict metrics using deterministic matching against fixed labels, eliminating need for inference-time judge models.
AI.result: With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM boosted Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks. Gains transferred to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures.
AI.conclusion: Structured rubric supervision through data synthesis frameworks like PRISM represents a scalable path toward improving multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following, enabling models to act as rubric executors rather than just question answerers.

title: ASGE-RR: Agentic Service Graph Embedding with Revisable Reservations for Dynamic AI-Agent Calls
summary:
AI-agent workflows often involve remote calls to models, memory stores, and tools distributed across a network. As execution progresses, these dependency calls collectively form an agentic service graph (ASG). Unlike traditional service requests, many dependency calls are revealed only at runtime. Consequently, allocating resources to a currently visible call may consume capacity later needed by a call from a higher-value workflow. We formulate this challenge as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem that maps runtime-revealed workflow calls to service replicas and network paths under capacity, cost and deadline constraints. We present ASGE-RR, an online ASGE controller with revisable reservations. ASGE-RR protects capacity for likely future calls while enforcing the constraints. ASGE-RR evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
  We evaluate ASGE-RR using OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows executed with gpt-5.6-luna and replayed over in two complementary experimental environments, a controlled Docker testbed and a WAN testbed. The investigation shows that all the evaluated AI-agent tasks expose at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that can be steered before connection establishment. Exploiting this control point, even though the experimental environments are small-scale, ASGE-RR already demonstrates noticeable potential: It completes (up to) 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed. The results suggest that runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity: protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time.

AI.tldr: ASGE-RR: An online controller that allocates resources for AI-agent workflows with runtime-revealed dependencies, using revisable reservations to protect capacity for likely future calls and improve workflow completion rates.
AI.motivation: AI-agent workflows involve remote calls to distributed models, memory stores, and tools that form an agentic service graph (ASG). Unlike traditional services, many dependency calls are only revealed at runtime, creating a challenge where allocating resources to current calls may consume capacity needed later by higher-value workflow calls.
AI.method: Formulate Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE) as an online network-control problem. Present ASGE-RR, an online controller with revisable reservations that maps runtime-revealed workflow calls to service replicas and network paths under capacity, cost, and deadline constraints. ASGE-RR protects capacity for likely future calls, evaluates candidate mappings against predicted workflow continuations, and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
AI.result: All evaluated AI-agent tasks expose at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that can be steered before connection establishment. ASGE-RR completes up to 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and current-call steering controller on WAN testbed. Even in small-scale experimental environments, ASGE-RR demonstrates noticeable potential for improving workflow completion rates.
AI.conclusion: Runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity where protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time, addressing the unique challenges of AI-agent service graphs with dynamic, runtime-revealed dependencies.

title: From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction
summary: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

AI.tldr: Machine learning models for stroke outcome prediction can use clinical guideline-based categorical encodings instead of continuous predictors without significantly sacrificing performance, making models more clinically interpretable.
AI.motivation: Clinical adoption of ML models for stroke outcome prediction is limited because model explanations don't align with clinicians' reasoning. A user study called for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs to make models more interpretable and useful in clinical practice.
AI.method: Compared standard gradient-boosted models (with continuous predictors) against fully categorised gradient-boosted models on a multi-centre European stroke registry. The categorised models used stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds to discretize continuous predictors into clinically meaningful categories across three treatment cohorts.
AI.result: Fully categorised models performed statistically indistinguishably from continuous models in two of three treatment cohorts, with only one cohort showing significant predictive accuracy drop. Global feature importance rankings remained consistent across all treatment groups.
AI.conclusion: Discretizing continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors and is a viable design choice for stroke outcome models, potentially increasing clinical adoption through better interpretability.

title: Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning
summary: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

AI.tldr: AuroSFT is a parameter-efficient framework for multi-task SFT that uses compact, mergeable adapters instead of full-model checkpoints to manage task-wise scheduling, achieving better accuracy with lower storage costs.
AI.motivation: Traditional multi-task SFT treats heterogeneous data as a single optimization problem, ignoring that different tasks peak at different times. msft addressed this with task-wise scheduling but stored full-model checkpoints, making transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy.
AI.method: AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only injected adapters. It uses task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback with adapter checkpoints instead of full models. Each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor, keeping updates linear, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into frozen projections.
AI.result: Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy compared to 59.85% for msft reference, and obtains higher accuracy on all five tested backbones.
AI.conclusion: AuroSFT provides an efficient framework for multi-task SFT that reduces storage and deployment costs while improving performance through compact, mergeable adapter states and task-wise scheduling.

title: DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data
summary: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

AI.tldr: DoctorAgents is an agentic AI framework that uses specialized LLM agents to autonomously construct and optimize clinical ML pipelines through reasoning-driven refinement rather than brute-force search, outperforming traditional AutoML methods.
AI.motivation: Clinical ML deployment is constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporally complex data. Developing effective ML pipelines for clinical data is time-consuming and error-prone. Existing AutoML systems rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory, making them inadequate for clinical settings.
AI.method: Reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. Propose DoctorAgents - an agentic AI framework with specialized LLM agents for generation, validation, and refinement that autonomously constructs end-to-end ML pipelines. Uses backpropagation of natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent for targeted updates without exhaustive search.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.
AI.conclusion: DoctorAgents represents a novel approach to clinical AutoML that shifts from brute-force search to reasoning-driven refinement, enabling more effective and interpretable ML pipeline development for complex clinical data.

title: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
summary: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILLTRACE is a multi-trace provenance auditing framework that detects LLM-agent skill reuse by analyzing expression, implementation, and operational traces, achieving high accuracy on benchmark tests and practical audit scenarios.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent ecosystems are growing with reusable skills (mixed-modality packages of metadata, instructions, code, tools, etc.). As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse requires new approaches beyond traditional code clone detection because evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure, making existing single-modality detectors inadequate.
AI.method: SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression Trace, Implementation Trace, and Operational Trace. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only in the initial Operational-trace extraction during ingestion. During audit, it compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports reuse decisions.
AI.result: On SKILLTRACE-BENCH with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 score 0.898. A wild audit of 36,446 skills demonstrates that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.
AI.conclusion: SKILLTRACE provides an effective multi-trace provenance auditing framework for detecting LLM-agent skill reuse across distributed evidence, addressing limitations of existing single-modality detectors and enabling practical auditing in growing marketplace ecosystems.

title: Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
summary: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

AI.tldr: AuroOFT enhances quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) by adding nonlinear corrections to enable better adaptation of low-bit language models while maintaining parameter efficiency.
AI.motivation: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models but is limited to linear orthogonal transformations, restricting input-dependent nonlinear corrections.
AI.method: AuroOFT keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. It maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes it functionally identical to qoft at initialization.
AI.result: AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA. The small math set is treated as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: AuroOFT successfully enhances qoft with nonlinear corrections while maintaining parameter efficiency and stability, achieving better performance than both qoft and QLoRA in quantized language model fine-tuning.

title: Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Multidisciplinary Applications
summary: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

AI.tldr: CANOE is a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that coordinates care plans through specialized agents generating arguments for interventions, resolving conflicts via argumentation frameworks, and allowing human contestation for transparent, safe clinical decision-making.
AI.motivation: Current monolithic LLM pipelines fail to transparently and safely synthesize heterogeneous clinical information across multiple disciplines for care plan coordination, lacking explainability and contestability.
AI.method: Five-module framework: 1) complexity assessment, 2) adaptive team recruitment, 3) role-based argumentative computation via Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), 4) human-in-the-loop contestation, and 5) care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting/attacking arguments, conflicts resolved through arena-based clash resolution, acceptability scores propagate across argumentation graph.
AI.result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG datasets using multiple metrics shows medically fine-tuned models achieve strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.
AI.conclusion: CANOE addresses limitations of monolithic LLMs for care plan coordination by providing transparent, contestable multi-agent decision-making with strong clinical correctness, safety, and explainability through neuro-symbolic argumentation.

title: Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application
summary: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

AI.tldr: Proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECR) to generalize from instance-level causal pairs to relation-level causal abstractions, with a system to distill AECRs from noisy data and a model to inject them into event prediction tasks for improved generalization on rare and unseen events.
AI.motivation: Existing instance-level causal event pairs suffer from poor generalization on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations, limiting the effectiveness of event-centric analytical systems for risk warning, decision support, and narrative understanding.
AI.method: 1) Proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECR) as a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm; 2) Designs multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system with similarity-constrained clustering to distill AECRs from noisy data; 3) Builds two complete AECR knowledge bases; 4) Proposes Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) that injects retrieved AECRs into causality Graph Event Prediction benchmark via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.
AI.result: Applying AECRs substantially strengthens generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples in quantitative experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed abstract causal knowledge framework (AECR) effectively addresses generalization deficits in event causal reasoning, demonstrating practical utility through improved performance on event prediction tasks, particularly for challenging rare and unseen event cases.

title: An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals
summary: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

AI.tldr: A fully functional, pre-deployment robo-advisor application that uses RL and NLP to provide personalized, tax-aware portfolio management for retail investors, integrating with live brokerage APIs.
AI.motivation: Retail investors lack access to personalized, tax-aware portfolio management available to institutional clients. Existing solutions are either too simplistic (static rule-based robo-advisors) or inaccessible (institutional systems with high minimums and complex tech stacks).
AI.method: A three-phase reinforcement learning system: 1) self-supervised cross-asset encoder, 2) Mixture-of-Experts allocation policy with learned intent router, 3) lightweight LoRA adapter for personalization from individual brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. Built as FastAPI backend + web dashboard with NLP interface.
AI.result: Functionally complete, integration-tested application against live brokerage API (Alpaca paper-trading), including multi-user auth, confirmation flow, email digests, and audit trail. Preliminary validation via 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals. System not yet deployed to real users.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a concrete path to deploy institutional-grade portfolio management to retail investors, reporting engineering lessons about integration challenges and the importance of end-to-end empirical verification for applied RL systems using live external data sources.

title: IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Dynamics at the Frontiers of Optimization, Sampling, and Games
summary: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

AI.tldr: IFlowNets extend generative flow networks to incomplete information games, fixing theoretical issues with prior approaches and showing competitive performance against CFR and RL methods.
AI.motivation: There's a gap in using generative sampling frameworks for incomplete information games, as most work blends RL with CFR methods. The authors want to extend Adversarial Flow Networks to incomplete information settings but found theoretical issues with existing constraints.
AI.method: Extended Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets) to incomplete information games, creating Information Flow Networks (IFNs). Proved previous constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadequate for obtaining valid densities and training objectives, and proposed a generalization that fixes these issues.
AI.result: IFlowNets strictly generalize AFlowNets and in preliminary tests on three standard game environments, they perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo CFR and standard RL-based methods in both performance and speed.
AI.conclusion: Information Flow Networks provide a valid generative sampling framework for incomplete information games that addresses theoretical limitations of previous approaches and shows promising empirical results compared to existing methods.

title: Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI
summary:
Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

AI.tldr: Otter is a 15.3M-parameter AI that predicts human chess moves by modeling play as a time-aware sequential process, achieving 55.23% top-1 accuracy with less parameters and data than prior models.
AI.motivation: Prior human chess models like Maia 2 treat positions in isolation, failing to capture that human chess is a time-aware, sequential activity influenced by move history and clock pressure.
AI.method: Uses a two-conditioning approach: (1) a move history encoder for the last 20 moves to capture opening preferences and behavioral tendencies, and (2) a time control module to account for clock pressure. Trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games.
AI.result: Achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move prediction accuracy, surpassing Maia 2 with far fewer parameters. Accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 Elo bracket. Model trained in 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
AI.conclusion: Modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches using smaller models, demonstrating the importance of temporal context in understanding human chess play.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction
summary: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction through systematic evaluation of 15 machine learning models, including TabPFN, with SHAP-based interpretability analysis and synthetic data augmentation to address limited training data.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from critical need for accurate post-wildfire debris-flow prediction to mitigate hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas, complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, need for model interpretability, and limited training data.
AI.method: The method involves: 1) Systematic evaluation of 15 machine learning models using basin-scale observations from western US; 2) Using repeated stratified cross-validation; 3) Applying SHAP for feature importance analysis; 4) Implementing synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address data scarcity; 5) Comparing model performance metrics including threat score.
AI.result: TabPFN achieves highest unaugmented performance with threat score of 0.637, closely followed by best tree-based models. SHAP analysis reveals short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation rank highest as predictive features, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. Synthetic augmentation improves performance of all models except CNN, with largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among deep learning models.
AI.conclusion: By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, demonstrating that TabPFN outperforms other models and synthetic data augmentation effectively addresses data scarcity challenges.

title: Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference
summary: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

AI.tldr: AutoThread: Adaptive thread-tuning for RL inference that uses a neural operator predictor guided by queueing theory to optimize thread counts dynamically, achieving significant speedup over existing methods.
AI.motivation: RL inference in simulation-in-the-loop systems faces performance bottlenecks due to simulator-side execution overhead and dynamic workloads that are sensitive to thread configurations. Existing multithreading strategies fail to properly match thread resources before or during execution, leading to resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput.
AI.method: Proposes AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method with three key components: 1) Uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor, 2) Incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide the predictions for fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads, and 3) Performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation.
AI.result: AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x compared to XGBoost and Reinforcer respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: AutoThread effectively addresses simulation bottlenecks in RL inference by combining predictive modeling with queueing theory constraints and online adaptation, providing significant performance improvements for dynamic workloads in simulation-in-the-loop systems.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics.
