We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

AI.tldr: Researchers create SearchAuditBench to evaluate LLM auditors' ability to diagnose and fix failures in deep search agents, and propose SearchAuditor framework that outperforms existing methods.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents are complex and fragile - small reasoning errors can propagate through long trajectories into incorrect answers. Manual diagnosis is difficult due to extremely long execution traces that may exceed human capacity.
AI.method: 1) Introduce SearchAuditBench benchmark with 1,243 failed trajectories from eight models on five search benchmarks, each annotated with error step, root cause, and repair reference. 2) Propose SearchAuditor - a multi-perspective auditing framework that localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication.
AI.result: Even strongest baseline with GPT-5.5 achieves only 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving 32.3% end-to-end pass rate. Using its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.
AI.conclusion: SearchAuditBench enables systematic evaluation of LLM auditors for deep search failures, and SearchAuditor demonstrates promising capability in diagnosing and repairing complex search-agent errors, reducing human burden in debugging these systems.

title: Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

AI.tldr: OSPDIM is a source-free online unsupervised domain adaptation framework that corrects geometric misalignment caused by label shifts in EEG-based BCIs by optimizing a manifold-constrained bias parameter via information maximization.
AI.motivation: Standard Riemannian alignment methods like RCT assume balanced class priors, but in realistic online BCI scenarios, label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing geometric misalignment of target data distributions. Existing offline methods rely on global batch statistics and cannot handle these dynamic, imbalanced data streams.
AI.method: Proposes OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), which introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping. This bias parameter is optimized via information maximization to correct geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly in a source-free online UDA framework.
AI.result: Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance.
AI.conclusion: OSPDIM offers a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems by effectively addressing label shifts on Riemannian manifolds in online settings, making it suitable for real-world BCI applications with dynamic, imbalanced data streams.

title: Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

AI.tldr: Meta-IRL latent context models underperform nonlinear shared rewards for Arctic shipping navigation, as vessel-specific variation is largely explained by observable features rather than hidden preferences.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted navigation in Arctic shipping needs interpretable and robust reward models that can adapt to changing sea-ice conditions. While meta-IRL methods with latent context variables aim to capture behavioral heterogeneity, it's unclear if these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode observable state information.
AI.method: Controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing three models: linear shared reward, nonlinear shared reward, and latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. Used behavioral analysis, context probes, and pre-registered feature-hiding ablation tests.
AI.result: Nonlinear reward improved held-out likelihood by 50.9% over linear baseline, but adding vessel-specific latent context reduced performance by 16.5%. Apparent vessel-level variation was largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Different evaluation metrics (predictive accuracy, route fidelity, reward transfer) yielded different model rankings.
AI.conclusion: Before adding per-vessel latent context in meta-IRL models, researchers should test whether observable route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation. This approach supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains by avoiding unnecessary complexity and potential overfitting.

title: PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

AI.tldr: PD-GS improves 3D Gaussian Splatting for talking heads by adding phoneme guidance to fix "leaky mouth" artifacts and improve lip articulation accuracy.
AI.motivation: 3DGS produces fast photorealistic talking heads but suffers from inaccurate lip articulation (over-smoothed motion, "leaky mouth" artifacts) because continuous acoustic embeddings under regression objectives bias predictions toward averaged mouth configurations, failing to capture brief discrete articulatory events like bilabial closures.
AI.method: Proposes Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS) which augments 3DGS with time-aligned phoneme tokens from ASR/forced-alignment. Core component is Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) that adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, preserving smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. Trained from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.
AI.result: On HDTF dataset, PD-GS achieves best lip geometry among baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, producing more linguistically faithful neural avatars with better lip articulation.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit time-aligned phoneme guidance into 3D Gaussian Splatting effectively addresses the "leaky mouth" problem by combining continuous audio-driven dynamics with discrete phonemic cues, leading to more accurate lip articulation that respects hard articulatory constraints while maintaining realistic motion.

title: QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures. The first four authors contributed equally
summary: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

AI.tldr: QEvict is a KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary eviction with recoverable eviction using three tiers (full precision, quantized recoverable, deleted) to preserve historical context while managing memory constraints in autoregressive LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Current KV-cache eviction methods have an irreversible problem: once tokens are evicted based on attention scores, they cannot become useful again even if future queries would find them important. This leads to permanently discarding states that later receive substantial attention.
AI.method: QEvict uses a three-tier system: 1) high-confidence windows kept in full precision, 2) intermediate windows stored in quantized recoverable tier, 3) lowest-confidence windows deleted. It uses cumulative attention scores to update window importance, and promotes quantized windows back to full precision when they become important again.
AI.result: QEvict consistently improves over existing eviction and quantization baselines across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks. It reduces missed attention and improves information retention under fixed memory budgets.
AI.conclusion: The recoverable eviction approach with quantization as an intermediate state effectively addresses the brittleness of current eviction policies, allowing tokens to regain importance as decoding progresses while managing memory constraints.

title: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
summary: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a comprehensive Agentic AI architecture for hospitals that addresses governance gaps and integration challenges to enable scalable AI deployment across clinical, operational, and financial domains.
AI.motivation: Most hospital AI deployments remain isolated point solutions in departmental silos, leading to duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints.
AI.method: The research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first Agentic AI architecture with three interoperable layers: (1) Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows, (2) Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code for regulatory standards, and (3) Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric incorporating federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into HIMS flows. Validation uses synthetic but realistic hospital data and open prototype implementation.
AI.result: The study demonstrates end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides hospital leaders with a pragmatic blueprint to transition from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, and cloud-native deployments.

title: When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

AI.tldr: SMRC-SD is a method for privileged distillation in multi-turn interactive agents that addresses state-reference mismatch by only applying distillation when the student's execution state matches reference states, and constructing state-conditioned teacher context.
AI.motivation: In interactive environments, students' actions change execution states, potentially reaching states not covered by reference trajectories. This creates state-reference mismatch when applying privileged distillation indiscriminately, making reference guidance unreliable for the actual states reached.
AI.method: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD) has two key components: 1) State-Matched Routing verifies whether student's current execution state matches a supported state along reference trajectory, applying distillation only at matched states; 2) Constructs state-conditioned teacher context from successful trajectories for each matched state.
AI.result: SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from 0.746 to 0.865 on ALFWorld and from 0.574 to 0.693 on WebShop. Ablations show both routing and context construction contribute to gains.
AI.conclusion: State-reference mismatch is a critical issue in privileged distillation for interactive agents. SMRC-SD effectively addresses this by selectively applying distillation only when student states match reference states and constructing state-compatible teacher context, leading to significant performance improvements.

title: DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting
summary: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

AI.tldr: DG-FedReuse is a federated learning mechanism that allows clients to reuse cached model updates when certain conditions are met, significantly reducing uplink communication costs with minimal accuracy trade-offs.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to reduce communication overhead in federated learning, which involves repeated local optimization and model-update transmission between clients and the server.
AI.method: DG-FedReuse uses age-decayed cached updates from selected clients when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy stays below a round-dependent threshold. It has hard cache-age limits, minimum fresh-client quotas, and uses adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation for fresh updates.
AI.result: At 90 rounds, DG-FedReuse achieves 83.36-85.42% uplink savings compared to 76.88% for Top-K FedAvg, with accuracy differences ranging from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. When considering symmetric dense-model-downlink, savings reduce to 41.68-42.71% with incremental gain of 3.24-4.27 percentage points over Top-K FedAvg.
AI.conclusion: The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in simulation but acknowledges limitations: it doesn't establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

title: Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour
comment: published as a conference paper at COLM'26
summary: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

AI.tldr: Small language models (0.6-1B parameters) fine-tuned on human behavioral data can match larger models (70B) for in-distribution tasks but require scale (up to 14B) for out-of-distribution generalization to novel task structures.
AI.motivation: To understand whether language models trained on human behavioral data actually process task structure or merely exploit statistical shortcuts, and to determine how model scale affects performance on both familiar and novel psychological tasks.
AI.method: Trained 14 models from 135M to 14B parameters across 4 architecture families on Psych-101 dataset (10.7M trial-level choices from 160 experiments). Used two diagnostics: 1) Progressively stripped four prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history) across 27 experiments, 2) Permuted trial order to test invariance.
AI.result: For in-distribution tasks, scale barely matters (0.6-1B parameters match 70B baseline). For out-of-distribution tasks, larger models show clear advantage in generalization. Masking stimuli/feedback content destroys 75.7% of learned information, showing choice history alone insufficient. Permutation reveals sensitivity to trial order when trials are interdependent.
AI.conclusion: Small cognitively fine-tuned models can serve as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments but remain bounded by training paradigms. They actually process task content rather than just relying on choice history, though generalization to novel structures requires scale.

title: Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics
summary: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

AI.tldr: Quantum-inspired world models using complex-valued and density-matrix-like representations show promise for local prediction but face limitations in long-horizon simulation compared to classical baselines.
AI.motivation: Most existing world models use classical representations (vectors, distributions, recurrent states, transformer activations), but the authors want to explore whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory (complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents) provide useful inductive biases for world modeling.
AI.method: Introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) - a quantum-inspired framework with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. Establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. Instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines.
AI.result: Complex-valued QSWMs show promising local predictive potential. However, both variants (complex-valued and density-matrix-like) reveal limitations in long-horizon rollout performance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired mathematical structures offer interesting inductive biases for world modeling with promising local predictive capabilities, but more work is needed to address long-horizon simulation challenges and fully realize their potential beyond classical approaches.

title: Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research
summary: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

AI.tldr: Project2Task: A graph-based planning system that converts research projects into well-structured, dependency-aware task portfolios for autonomous research agents.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous research systems treat projects as single oversized tasks or produce vague/overlapping tasks, lacking proper project-level planning with bounded tasks, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequencing.
AI.method: Represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms in directed lineage graphs, uses Bernoulli block-model objective to select portfolio decompositions, generates bounded tasks with ownership, repairs overlaps, and creates dependency-aware task contracts.
AI.result: Achieves average quality score of 7.15 vs 4.58 (Brief Baseline) and 5.31 (Topic-only); integration with AutoResearchClaw increases task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759.
AI.conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning produces coherent, non-redundant, executable research-task portfolios, demonstrating value for autonomous research systems.

title: Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models
summary: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

AI.tldr: A provable pipeline for learning compact linear state-space representations of nonlinear dynamical systems through convex learning and distillation, without solving non-convex system identification.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of learning nonlinear dynamical systems without solving difficult non-convex system-identification problems. Current methods lack provable end-to-end guarantees for extracting linear dynamical system (LDS) representations from nonlinear dynamics.
AI.method: Two-step pipeline: 1) Learn implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method competing with best linear observers. 2) Apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert predictor into explicit recurrent linear dynamical system.
AI.result: Main theorem shows average prediction error decomposes into exponentially-small distillation term plus OSF learning term governed by Luenberger complexity. Guarantee is dimension-free (depends on observer complexity rather than latent dimension). Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show pipeline produces compact LDS predictors matching or outperforming directly trained baselines.
AI.conclusion: Provides first end-to-end provable method for extracting best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation, enabling compact linear representations of complex nonlinear systems.

title: TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation
summary: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

AI.tldr: TriQua is an LLM factuality evaluation framework that adaptively models facts as either standard triples (simple claims) or hyperrelational facts with qualifiers (complex claims), enabling precise verification with contextual preservation.
AI.motivation: The decompose-then-verify paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation has a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts (single sentences) often omit essential context, while broader statements lack granularity needed for precise assessment. Current approaches struggle to balance context preservation with verification granularity.
AI.method: TriQua flexibly models facts based on their complexity - simple claims are extracted as standard triples (subject-predicate-object), while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves necessary context without sacrificing atomicity. The framework includes TriQuaScore to quantify factuality of structured fact units, and directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show: 1) TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, 2) TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and 3) It outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.
AI.conclusion: TriQua successfully addresses the context-granularity trade-off in LLM factuality evaluation through adaptive fact modeling (triples vs. hyperrelational facts), enabling more precise, context-aware verification with fine-grained error detection and quantification via TriQuaScore.

title: Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples
summary: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

AI.tldr: A method that identifies spurious correlation samples after model convergence by analyzing prediction fragility to input perturbations, enabling worst-group accuracy improvements without requiring group annotations or early-stopping decisions.
AI.motivation: Models trained on data with spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy but fail on minority groups where the correlation doesn't hold. Existing methods require identifying early training signals and group-labeled validation data for hyperparameter selection, creating practical deployment barriers.
AI.method: After model convergence, analyze prediction fragility by applying fixed perturbations to inputs. Samples consistent with spurious correlation are classified by shared rules (robust), while minority samples are fit through input-specific configurations (fragile). The method detects fragile samples that flip predictions more often under perturbation, requiring only two forward passes per sample.
AI.result: The method raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8% without any group annotations, compared to 85.8% with ground-truth group labels. It outperforms methods requiring early-stopping epoch decisions and validation group annotations.
AI.conclusion: Spurious correlation samples can be effectively identified after convergence by analyzing prediction fragility to perturbations, enabling practical improvements to worst-group accuracy without the need for group annotations or early-stopping decisions.

title: Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation
summary: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

AI.tldr: DSV system transforms written dream descriptions into coherent four-panel image sequences using LLM for temporal splitting and text-to-image models with quality control regeneration.
AI.motivation: Dreams are emotionally intense but difficult to communicate effectively in written form; visual representations could help convey dream experiences more vividly and intuitively.
AI.method: 1) Use large language model to split dream descriptions into four chronological parts; 2) Generate images for each part using text-to-image model; 3) Maintain visual coherence across sequence; 4) Regenerate images that don't match text well; 5) Evaluate using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL models on 50 dream visualizations from DreamBank.
AI.result: Developed DSV system capable of creating temporal four-panel image sequences from dream descriptions, with evaluation showing results in quality, fidelity, and coherence metrics measured objectively using vision-language models.
AI.conclusion: DSV provides an effective method for visualizing dreams through sequential images, bridging the gap between emotional dream experiences and communicable representations using modern AI models.

title: Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

AI.tldr: Search2Skill is a framework that enables LLM-based agents to automatically identify capability gaps, search external sources for professional knowledge, and distill retrieved information into reusable structured skills using rubric-based reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods are limited to the model's existing parametric knowledge or trajectories, but real-world professional skills and domain conventions often lie beyond what the model already knows and are hard to elicit from the agent alone.
AI.method: Search2Skill framework with three key components: 1) automatically identifies agent's capability gaps, 2) searches external sources to address these gaps, and 3) distills retrieved evidence into structured reusable skills. It's optimized through a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.
AI.result: Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Additional analyses reveal gains come from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and acquired skills transfer across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Search2Skill provides an effective framework for LLM-based agents to evolve beyond their initial knowledge boundaries by learning structured reusable skills from external sources, enabling better performance in expert domains through automated knowledge acquisition and skill distillation.

title: Why the Third Axis Is Freedom
comment: Experiment code available on GitHub, in the papers folder: https://github.com/ViscousLemming/Technical-Appendices
summary: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Explorative Modeling (XM) uses K outputs per comparison, claiming to explore generative expressivity, but the paper argues the real 'third pretraining axis' is freedom (weakness of behavioral constraints), which better explains XM's benefits and generalization.
AI.motivation: Traditional generative training compares single outputs, favoring models that produce common answers over those with broader repertoires. XM proposes using K outputs per comparison as an "exploration" axis, but the paper argues the underlying mechanism is actually about selecting for model freedom (weak behavioral constraints) rather than exploration per se.
AI.method: The paper provides formal proof that average XM loss depends on the probability of missing acceptable regions, with exploration raising miss probability to power K. It demonstrates empirically that XM optimizes for freedom through Forward XM experiments measuring how K affects freedom, and by training XM candidate pools and comparing validation selection with a freedom selector using unlabeled parent contexts.
AI.result: For K>1, match probability rises with freedom. Larger K increased or saturated measured freedom in experiments, and increased freedom under context-dependent targets. In validation selection comparisons, freedom-based selection won in 29 out of 30 cases against standard XM validation.
AI.conclusion: Generative expressivity is a proxy for freedom that discards important extension structure. XM is a means to select for freedom, which is the actual end goal. Selecting for freedom improves XM performance under distribution shift, and freedom is the proper "third pretraining axis" associated with better generalization.

title: LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs
summary: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

AI.tldr: LUNAR is the first benchmark for evaluating LLM personalization using longitudinal app interaction histories across daily-life domains, revealing that behavioral data access is necessary but insufficient, with evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities.
AI.method: LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns to construct a benchmark from longitudinal app interaction histories across domains (clothing, food, housing, mobility), addressing data sparsity and privacy concerns.
AI.result: Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show: 1) Behavioral logs are necessary but insufficient for deep personalization; 2) Neither more context nor larger models guarantee better performance; 3) Effective personalization depends on selecting/integrating relevant evidence across domains; 4) Direct retrieval outperforms compressed memory; 5) Stronger personalization conflicts with privacy protection.
AI.conclusion: Evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control are identified as key challenges for personalized LLMs, with LUNAR providing a foundation for evaluating cross-domain behavioral personalization.

title: EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

AI.tldr: EvoHarness-RL enables LLM agents to learn policies for managing external execution harnesses, allowing selective state access and coordination during long-horizon tasks, achieving 96.9% success in ALFWorld.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents need external execution support for state management, progress tracking, tool invocation, and experience reuse, but current approaches require manual engineering of harness policies and state management.
AI.method: EvoHarness-RL introduces Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as harness state. Uses supervised harness fine-tuning to teach harness action space construction, followed by cost-aware GRPO to learn coordination policies for selective state access during long-horizon interactions.
AI.result: Achieves 96.9% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-8B LLM. Reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing (internalizing patterns into model policy) and harness evolution (refining harness into compact, task-adaptive state substrate).
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, moving beyond just adding stronger tools or larger memories. This enables more selective and efficient external-state access during task execution.

title: WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order by given name
summary: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

AI.tldr: WorldClaw: An agent-based framework for generating large-scale, editable 3D worlds from open-ended text prompts using hierarchical planning and refinement.
AI.motivation: Generating large-scale 3D worlds from text is challenging because systems must maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit editable assets simultaneously for downstream use.
AI.method: A fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework where planning agents translate text into structured specifications of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. It builds globally coherent terrain from semantic layouts, reusable assets, and region-aware height fields. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable meshes, and recovers placements, with render-based agents refining terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.
AI.result: WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while maintaining consistent global terrain structure across diverse open-world prompts.
AI.conclusion: WorldClaw demonstrates an effective agent-based approach for open-world 3D scene generation that addresses the joint challenges of global coherence, local detail, and asset editability through hierarchical planning and refinement.

title: Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty
summary: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

AI.tldr: HProbZ is a neural network output head that separates prediction uncertainty into three distinct sources (binary mode choice, bounded systematic drift, and stochastic noise) using a zonotope representation, enabling single-pass future prediction refinement and providing both analytic risk assessment and conformal sets.
AI.motivation: Existing probabilistic prediction heads (Gaussian mixtures or single conformal regions) fail to separate distinct sources of uncertainty present in real prediction tasks: discrete mode choices, bounded systematic drift within modes, and irreducible stochastic noise.
AI.method: Introduces Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ) - an output head representing three uncertainty sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, with closed-form likelihood via convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, allowing single forward pass refinement.
AI.result: Proves that the three generators are identifiable from likelihood up to permutation, and HProbZ densities are representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. Provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference. Empirical results show effectiveness compared to same-encoder mixture baselines.
AI.conclusion: HProbZ offers structural properties that neither mixture nor convex-conformal predictors jointly provide, effectively separating different uncertainty sources while enabling efficient multi-step prediction refinement and risk assessment.

title: Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty
summary: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

AI.tldr: A new optimization engine (CEV and RobustCEV) for military pre-commitment posture planning that outperforms greedy baselines by considering geographic coverage and adversarial threats through scenario-weighted optimization and Bayesian game theory.
AI.motivation: Current military asset placement practices use greedy heuristics that maximize strategic value but ignore geographic coverage, making them vulnerable to adversaries targeting high-value locations. This leaves a critical gap in joint operational planning.
AI.method: Modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. Developed Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency, and RobustCEV extension that iterates against a Bayesian adversary updating targeting distribution in response to placement.
AI.result: In Indo-Pacific basing experiments: (1) greedy baseline suffers 25.1% efficiency penalty and 57.3% readiness collapse under adversarial threat; (2) CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy; (3) RobustCEV recovers up to 158% efficiency against adaptive adversaries using deceptive threat priors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scenario-weighted robust optimization framework significantly outperforms current greedy approaches by addressing geographic coverage and adversarial threats, validated through statistical analysis confirming performance gaps are structural properties of placement strategies.

title: Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers
summary: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

AI.tldr: Standard multi-head attention has fixed linear projections that don't adapt to input contexts, limiting its ability to represent complex permutation-invariant set functions. MZAttn introduces adaptive matrix-zonotope value projections that can better represent high-rank, combinatorially complex targets.
AI.motivation: Current multi-head attention uses input-dependent softmax routing but input-independent linear value projections, creating an asymmetry that limits its ability to represent complex permutation-invariant set targets. This architectural limitation is particularly problematic for functions requiring input-dependent processing beyond just routing.
AI.method: Introduces Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) as a complexity measure for set operators. Proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) which replaces fixed value projections with context-adaptive matrix-zonotope families: a center matrix plus sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The method preserves permutation equivariance and reduces to standard attention at initialization.
AI.result: Theoretical depth-separation analysis shows standard attention needs depth proportional to target's TDOF, while single-layer MZAttn can represent the same targets. Experiments show MZAttn's advantage is selective - significant on high-rank, sparsely combinatorial targets, but minimal on aggregate-statistic targets where standard attention already performs well.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetry in multi-head attention's routing vs. value projection limits its expressivity for complex set functions. MZAttn provides a more expressive alternative that adapts to input context, offering architectural advantages for targets requiring high TDOF while maintaining compatibility with standard attention initialization.

title: OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality
summary: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

AI.tldr: OrchestraBench is a benchmark that evaluates multi-agent orchestration failures, recovery, and decomposition through controlled failure injection, revealing different failure-handling tiers and showing that intent-reasoning routing outperforms keyword/flag routing on adversarial cases.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent orchestration benchmarks typically only report task accuracy without diagnosing why pipelines fail, where cascades begin, or which routing decisions cause breakdowns, leaving a gap in understanding failure mechanisms and recovery strategies.
AI.method: OrchestraBench uses a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery metrics, compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests, and conducts controlled mechanism probes with real Claude agents over verifiable arithmetic dependency chains.
AI.result: Intent-reasoning model router scored 100% on adversarial cases vs. 0% for keyword/flag router. Three failure-handling tiers identified: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation partially (0.30), and latent/semantic modes never recovered (0.0). Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). Blind retry reproduced latent faults, and trusted-state repair gains came mainly from trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection.
AI.conclusion: Detection and attribution are necessary for failure containment, cascade radius increases with pipeline depth, and apparent containment gains from trusted-state repair primarily come from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection mechanisms.

title: KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Zhaowei Han and Xiang Zhang contributed equally to this work. Code: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill
summary: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

AI.tldr: KV-Skill introduces external factorized operators that frozen language models read through a lightweight interface, enabling task knowledge to be stored separately from weights or prompt text, improving efficiency and modularity.
AI.motivation: Current task knowledge storage has limitations: text in prompts must be interpreted on every use (inefficient), while weight adaptation makes capabilities difficult to load, remove, or share independently. There's a need for modular task knowledge storage that doesn't require constant text interpretation or weight modifications.
AI.method: KV-Skill uses external factorized operators with two complementary paths: 1) Registration converts text skills into text-derived operators and trains a shared per-backbone interface; 2) Reward learning develops compact latent operators directly from task outcomes. The approach uses a lightweight interface for frozen language models without adding positions to the prompt.
AI.result: Across ten benchmarks and four backbones: text-to-KV-Skill consistently improves procedural knowledge effectiveness; On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration achieves 77.2% accuracy vs 23.4% for source text and 64.5% for SoftSkill; Under matched budgets, KV-Skill outperforms soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA in 7/8 settings; Text-derived operators retain benefits with one task-aligned direction per layer; One shared interface supports three independently loadable KV-Skills without forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Task knowledge can be effectively acquired from text or experience, compressed into external operators, and deployed separately from the backbone, offering a modular and efficient alternative to text-based prompting and weight adaptation approaches.

title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

AI.tldr: A benchmark and trace-logging framework evaluates agent architectures for microscopy control, finding benchmarks useful for direct comparisons but insufficient for predicting performance on unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly used to control scientific instruments like microscopes, there's a lack of established engineering paradigms. Researchers need to make many design choices and want agents that can both perform known tasks and generalize to new ones.
AI.method: Developed a benchmark and trace-logging framework to evaluate agent architectures. Tested one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. Analyzed 105 configurations, 1,949 test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals.
