AI.result: Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure modes between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results failed to reliably predict performance on new, unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite doesn't support a task-independent global configuration model for predicting performance on unseen tasks.

title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
summary: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

AI.tldr: Align-RAG is a training-free method for retrieval-augmented time series forecasting that applies closed-form amplitude and phase alignment to retrieved examples before feeding them to frozen time series foundation models, outperforming trained adapters without any parameter learning.
AI.motivation: Current retrieval-augmented forecasting methods rely on learned fusion modules/trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into backbone forecasts, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. The authors challenge this unnecessary assumption.
AI.method: Align-RAG applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. The method has no learned parameters and works by aligning retrieved examples with the query through amplitude and phase adjustments.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on frozen Chronos-Bolt across all seven datasets in standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE). Improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning.
AI.conclusion: Frozen time series foundation models already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals. Closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module training. The gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without training.

title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
summary:
CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

AI.tldr: CASCADE predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbations using ARACNe networks via MCP. The study validates predictions against real tumor data, showing strong accuracy for proliferation regulators like MYC but inconsistent results for other gene types, and benchmarks LLM agents for natural language to tool call conversion.
AI.motivation: Previous validation methods only check if predicted genes are known cancer genes (membership), but this study aims to test if the predicted direction of gene expression change matches reality, providing a more rigorous validation approach.
AI.method: Used focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for knockdown experiments against TCGA patient tumor data. Validated predictions by comparing direction of change between amplified vs non-amplified tumors. Applied Fisher's exact test against MSigDB gene-set baselines and benchmarked LLM-based agents on natural language to tool call conversion.
AI.result: For MYC, predictions showed strong concordance across BRCA (90.0%), COAD (72.0%), and STAD (85.7%) cancers. Results replicated in METABRIC cohort (87.2%). However, validation success was gene-specific: proliferation regulators mostly replicated while lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 consistently failed. LLM agents achieved 71.4-85.7% exact match on tool calls but had issues with ambiguous queries.
AI.conclusion: CASCADE shows promising predictive accuracy for specific gene types (proliferation regulators) but not universal applicability. Current validation methods may be insufficient for comprehensive benchmarking. LLM agents work well for straightforward queries but struggle with ambiguity, suggesting need for improved prompt engineering or validation strategies.

title: LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction
summary: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

AI.tldr: LC-GRPO introduces Langevin correction to flow-based GRPO methods, aligning stochastic training rollouts with deterministic test-time ODE inference by combining ODE Euler steps with score-based stochastic corrections.
AI.motivation: Flow-based generative models use deterministic ODEs at inference but require stochastic rollouts for RL training. Existing methods use SDEs which create distribution mismatch between training (blurry SDE samples) and test-time (sharp ODE samples), harming policy optimization.
AI.method: LC-GRPO adds Langevin correction to each rollout transition: first takes ODE Euler step aligned with inference, then applies stochastic Langevin correction targeting marginal distribution using flow velocity (no extra score model). Transition remains isotropic Gaussian with tractable likelihood.
AI.result: Theoretically shows one Langevin correction reduces Wasserstein error of imperfect ODE Euler step. At matched randomness, transition more accurate than standard Euler-Maruyama SDE discretization. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, HunyuanVideo show improved reward optimization, preserved quality, and narrowed training-test gap.
AI.conclusion: LC-GRPO effectively bridges stochastic training and deterministic inference in flow-based GRPO, improving reward optimization while maintaining generation quality across image and video tasks.

title: Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models
summary: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that GPT-3.5 can be effectively used for counterfactual analysis in online lending, achieving predictive performance close to advanced ML algorithms through prompt engineering, and demonstrates logical coherence in generating counterfactual ROIs.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual analysis is valuable for decision-making but traditional methods may be complex; the authors want to explore whether large language models like GPT-3.5 can serve as effective tools for counterfactual analysis, specifically in online lending contexts where evaluating different interest rate schemes is crucial.
AI.method: The study uses GPT-3.5 for counterfactual analysis in online lending, first assessing its predictive performance compared with advanced machine learning algorithms (including gradient-boosted regression), employing prompt engineering techniques, and then using GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rates to evaluate its logical coherence and causal reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: Prompt engineering significantly improved GPT's predictive performance from 1.97% to 2.84% R-squared, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression; GPT exhibited logical coherence and causal reasoning in generating counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rate scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Large language models like GPT-3.5 have significant potential as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, with broader applications in various predictive and decision-making contexts, demonstrating that with proper prompt engineering, they can achieve performance comparable to specialized machine learning algorithms while maintaining logical coherence.

title: GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification
summary: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification that modulates fine-grained evidence units rather than entire modalities, improving reliability when some modalities are missing.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal classification methods assume all modalities are available, but real-world inputs often have missing modalities. Current imputation and dynamic fusion methods operate at a coarse modality level and cannot separate reliable from misleading components within recovered modalities, compromising prediction reliability.
AI.method: GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs as fine-grained evidence units. It computes counterfactual effects by scoring what happens when replacing each unit with a reference representation using prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores in one forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates and converted to additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering backbone architecture.
AI.result: Experiments across six benchmarks show GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to exact counterfactual effects.
AI.conclusion: GAUGE establishes a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness, enabling more reliable multimodal classification when inputs are incomplete.

title: Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs
summary: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

AI.tldr: A three-stream detector combining motion with restricted state views improves reasoning validity detection over displacement-only methods, showing reasoning correctness is better read from state-conditioned motion than static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.
AI.motivation: As language models are increasingly used for verifiable reasoning tasks, reliably distinguishing sound from flawed reasoning has become crucial. Current trajectory-based methods use layerwise residual-stream displacements but omit state context, while full-state approaches risk reintroducing shortcut-prone information.
AI.method: Proposed a three-stream detector combining motion with two restricted views of location: 1) a coarse region reader based on vector quantization, and 2) a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This restores enough state context to interpret motion without returning to full-state probing.
AI.result: On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, the method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over displacement-only state-of-the-art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also performs well on factual completion and fact verification tasks, outperforming all compared detectors.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone. Motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals, and the method places the signal on correctness rather than on a specific kind of reasoning.

title: C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

AI.tldr: C³PO benchmark reveals MLLMs suffer from modality dominance bias, failing at cross-modal reasoning despite multimodal perception
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs can process multiple sensory inputs but exhibit brittle cross-modal reasoning with heavy bias toward dominant modalities, limiting their robustness
AI.method: Created C³PO benchmark with 3,404 samples across video, audio, image, and text using 25 logically grounded templates; evaluated information composition and counterfactual conflict; used attention probes to analyze failures
AI.result: Best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) achieved 73.17% accuracy vs human 88.64%; 86-95% failures due to modality dominance; open-source models collapse under conflict; 56-point gap between templates shows performance depends on structural roles
AI.conclusion: Multimodal perception doesn't guarantee robust reasoning; architectures need sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature modality dominance and enable reliable cross-modal inference

title: Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics
summary: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

AI.tldr: PMOT introduces a potential-flow framework for general p-cost optimal transport that parameterizes velocity fields with scalar potentials and trains them using self-induced matching loss along straight bridges.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for a general framework for optimal transport with arbitrary p-cost functions (c_p(x,y)=||x-y||^p), moving beyond the classical p=2 case to handle a wider range of transport problems.
AI.method: PMOT parameterizes continuous normalizing flow (CNF) velocity fields with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou-Brenier form for exponent p. It trains the potential gradient using self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching.
AI.result: The main theoretical result establishes zero-loss exactness: under regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou-Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding p-optimal transport map and dynamics. Experimental results show PMOT learns p-specific maps agreeing with OT references, remains competitive as a density model on high-dimensional data, and demonstrates flexible terminal matching.
AI.conclusion: PMOT provides a principled potential-flow framework for general p-cost optimal transport that theoretically recovers optimal maps and demonstrates practical effectiveness across synthetic benchmarks, density modeling, and sample-based matching tasks.

title: When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering
summary: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

AI.tldr: Study finds that agreement across perturbed inputs (re-rendered scientific figures) correlates with correctness in VLMs, but using agreement as self-training target reduces accuracy by eliminating error diversity.
AI.motivation: To directly measure the coupling between model agreement across perturbed inputs and correctness, which is typically assumed in natural image settings but hard to verify without exact ground truth.
AI.method: Built RENDEQ generator to create render-equivalence sets of scientific figures where images are semantically equivalent by construction; measured agreement-correctness coupling across three VLMs using three independent instantiations.
AI.result: Re-rendering beats resampling on accuracy/reliability; agreement generally beats token probability baseline; main dispersion source is plotting library; fine-tuning on cross-render consensus reduces accuracy (opposite of natural image results).
AI.conclusion: Agreement certifies correctness only above threshold set by error diffuseness; optimizing for agreement destroys that diffuseness, explaining why self-training fails on this controlled dataset.

title: Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index
comment: This paper has already been accepted and presented at the IEEE 27th International Conference on Information Reuse and Integration for Data Science (IRI 2026) from July 31 to August 2, 2026, in Seattle, WA, USA
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

AI.tldr: PSI is a new metric that evaluates if LLM tutoring responses match learner readiness and curriculum progression, not just correctness, and can be used to improve weak responses.
AI.motivation: Current LLM tutor evaluations focus mainly on answer quality but fail to measure instructional fit - whether responses match the learner's current foundation, course sequence, and timing of concept introduction.
AI.method: Created PSI (Pedagogical Suitability Index) as a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores to evaluate LLM tutoring responses. Evaluated four LLM tutors across 240 scenario-based evaluations using both standard and defective prompts, then applied PSI-guided regeneration to 62 weak-performing cases.
AI.result: Baseline PSI scores across four models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) ranged from 0.557 to 0.638 with no clear separation between open-weight and closed models. PSI-guided feedback substantially improved 51 of 62 weak cases (82.3%). Manual evaluation showed PSI-identified weaknesses were instructionally meaningful and improvements aligned with human judgment.
AI.conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment matters more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and such alignment is both measurable through PSI and improvable using PSI-guided feedback.

title: Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading
summary: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an equivariance-based reliability measure for vision-language models that complements invariance testing, revealing systematic misreadings that traditional perturbation methods miss.
AI.motivation: Current label-free reliability methods for vision-language models rely on invariance (answers shouldn't change with perturbations), but this has a blind spot where systematic misreadings survive perturbations and get certified as correct incorrectly.
AI.method: The paper proposes using equivariance instead: when input data is edited, correct answers should change by predictable amounts. The authors develop mathematical formalism showing errors are invisible when transformations commute with the error, and they characterize completeness of edit suites for different error types (affine reading errors, label permutations). They implement this as Equivariance-Consistency Score.
AI.result: They create REND-EQUIV with matched invariance/equivariance sets, show predicted ordering holds across three models, demonstrate a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, and show cyclic relabeling delivers predicted gains. They explain why previous classifier metamorphic-testing literature saw ordering inversions.
AI.conclusion: Detectability is a joint property of the relation and fault class, not of the relation alone. Equivariance complements invariance for more complete reliability assessment of vision-language models, revealing systematic errors that traditional methods miss.

title: Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation
summary: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

AI.tldr: Workshop study shows mixed stakeholders (community, police, academics) broadly accept AI in policing except for recidivism risk assessment, with racial bias concerns leading to fundamental questions about effectiveness, benefit distribution, and equity.
AI.motivation: AI adoption in policing is increasing globally with known racial bias risks, yet affected communities are rarely included in decision-making about AI implementation in law enforcement contexts.
AI.method: Conducted a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop with 30 participants (community representatives, police officers, academics) to assess risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, explicitly focusing on racial bias.
AI.result: Participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright (most notably recidivism risk assessment). Discussions revealed that foregrounding racial equity didn't narrow deliberation but instead led to fundamental questions about tool effectiveness, genuine benefit delivery, and equitable benefit distribution.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating racial bias lens from the outset in AI risk-benefit analysis leads to more holistic assessments, similar to inclusive design's curb-cut effect, benefiting all stakeholders by addressing fundamental questions about effectiveness and equity.

title: SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning
summary: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

AI.tldr: SEAM is a framework that checks whether local scientific explanations from machine learning models can be combined into globally consistent explanations, detecting inconsistencies and attributing failures to specific components.
AI.motivation: Current scientific machine learning only validates models at local levels (subdomains, single predictions), but lacks methods to verify whether these local explanations can be assembled into globally admissible scientific explanations.
AI.method: SEAM uses a finite explanation-sheaf instantiation (SEAM-Ω) that represents regions with structured explanations having state, closure, and observation channels. It compares neighboring explanations on overlaps, converts disagreements into channel-resolved obstructions, and tests repair possibilities while monitoring distribution shifts.
AI.result: Across 19 experiments with synthetic PDE systems and Fourier neural operators, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. The framework establishes theorems for minimum-cost intervention and detectability.
AI.conclusion: SEAM provides a global explanation-consistency audit for existing solvers and learning models, addressing the critical gap between local validation and global scientific coherence in machine learning explanations.

title: SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications
summary: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

AI.tldr: Selective translation framework for natural language to formal specifications with abstention when unreliable, using conformal prediction and dual reliability signals to guarantee bounded error rates.
AI.motivation: Current translation models generate specifications for every input even when unreliable, creating safety risks in critical applications. Need for systems that can recognize when generated specifications may not be trustworthy.
AI.method: Proposed selective translation framework with two complementary black-box reliability signals: (1) fidelity of specification back-translation to natural language, (2) dispersion of repeated translations under semantic equivalence. Uses conformal risk control to calibrate scores into accept/abstain decisions with distribution-free error bounds, plus conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings for out-of-distribution screening.
AI.result: Demonstrated improved translation reliability, robustness under cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention across three formal specification languages: Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL).
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize unreliable specifications, with formal guarantees on error rates for safety-critical applications.

title: Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery
summary: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

AI.tldr: Self-supervised method (SAP) uses spectral aliasing to pretrain Transformers on unlabeled vibration data, enabling effective fault diagnosis with minimal labeled data.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for fault diagnosis requires extensive labeled data, which is scarce in industrial settings where obtaining labeled vibration data is difficult.
AI.method: Propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP): deliberately undersample vibration signals to create folded spectrum (aliasing), then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum as a self-supervised pretext task.
AI.result: SAP learns stable, highly discriminative representations on CWRU dataset. Linear probing with SAP achieves very high classification with minimal labeled data and low variance, outperforming full fine-tuning and fully supervised training.
AI.conclusion: SAP with linear probing is more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data, avoiding potentially destructive augmentations while learning frequency-domain invariants.

title: Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Equal contribution among Y. Chen, J. Jiang, and T. Shi (alphabetical order)
summary: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

AI.tldr: The paper studies optimal instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem and proves it can be reduced to a deterministic problem on prerequisite order ideals, with computational complexity ranging from polynomial-time solvable in some cases to NP-hard in others.
AI.motivation: When students need to learn concepts with prerequisite dependencies, the ordering of instruction matters for learning efficiency, but finding the optimal sequencing is computationally challenging due to stochastic learning outcomes and complex dependencies between concepts.
AI.method: The authors formulate instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem where attempting a concept succeeds with state-dependent probability. They prove this stochastic problem collapses exactly to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals. They analyze computational complexity via reductions from feedback arc set in tournaments and provide polynomial-time exact dynamic programming for cases with fixed prerequisite width.
AI.result: The stochasticity can be eliminated exactly without changing optimal values/actions. Optimal sequencing is NP-hard in general but polynomial-time solvable when transfer preferences remain acyclic with prerequisites or with fixed prerequisite width. A diagnostic mΔ bounds sequencing value before optimization. Empirical analysis on 70,893 CS course interactions shows the diagnostic certifies an easy regime, while constructed instances demonstrate challenging regimes where myopic sequencing suffers large regret but A* with consistent heuristic expands linearly many states.
AI.conclusion: Instructional sequencing complexity depends crucially on structure: while stochasticity can be eliminated, combinatorial complexity remains, with practical regimes ranging from trivial to computationally challenging. The diagnostic mΔ helps identify when optimization is worthwhile, and efficient algorithms exist for structured cases, providing theoretical foundations for practical instructional design.

title: CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits
summary: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

AI.tldr: CircuitSteer: A framework using Sparse Autoencoders to identify and manipulate multi-layer semantic circuits for more effective LLM steering, outperforming single-layer methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition rely on fixed single-layer interventions from aggregate activation differences, which impose uniform interventions across diverse inputs and fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers.
AI.method: Uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. Constructs feature flow circuits based on feature co-activation and geometric alignment of decoder directions, isolates multi-layer subcircuits for target behaviors, synthesizes dense steering vectors from sparse features, and applies multi-point interventions.
AI.result: Evaluated on toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal tasks across multiple model families. CircuitSteer consistently produced fluency-preserving interventions while competing methods either sacrificed text quality or failed on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with geometric alignment of features provides more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions for LLM alignment.

title: Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
summary: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

AI.tldr: RST is a recursive framework that synthesizes high-quality, long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale and low cost, with task difficulty increasing dramatically over rounds, enabling effective training of terminal agents.
AI.motivation: High-quality training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce (hundreds to thousands of dollars per task) due to the need for consistency between instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier. Human authoring doesn't scale, and direct LLM generation often breaks these dependencies.
AI.method: Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST) framework that starts from verified seed tasks, then recursively: extends reference solutions, realigns verifiers and instructions to new workflows, validates results in fresh sandboxes, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds.
AI.result: Produced 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at ~$0.05 per task over 15 rounds. Task difficulty increased substantially: median reference solution grew from 67 to 374 lines, executed commands from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 dropped from 90% to 2.5%. Fine-tuning on trajectories from these tasks improved models by up to 10 points on benchmarks, with PPO achieving relative gains of 20-41% over base models.
AI.conclusion: RST enables scalable, cost-effective generation of high-quality terminal-agent training data with increasing difficulty, showing no ceiling after 15 rounds and providing significant performance improvements for terminal agents when used for training.

title: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

AI.tldr: CvLoss is a plug-in structural regularizer that improves multivariate time series forecasting by constraining forecast residuals on cross-variable graphs to address dependencies among future values.
AI.motivation: Existing forecasting models focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations but largely ignore dependencies among future values. The Direct Forecasting paradigm uses point-wise objectives that don't explicitly constrain cross-variable structure, creating an objective gap when cross-variable and lagged dependencies exist.
AI.method: Proposes Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. It penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions.
AI.result: CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with various forecasting backbones. It addresses the objective gap in multivariate time series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly constraining cross-variable structure in forecasts through a graph-based residual regularizer, CvLoss effectively bridges the objective gap in multivariate forecasting and enhances model performance while maintaining compatibility with existing architectures.

title: Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability
summary: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the reliability of auditing autonomous data analysis agents that detect errors by comparing operations against sound analyses, quantifying error spread, controlling false positive rates, and establishing fundamental limits on error attribution.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents perform entire data analyses with minimal supervision, but when errors occur, it's unclear how to reliably determine which operation caused them. While recent methods audit by comparing to sound analyses, the reliability of such audits hasn't been studied.
AI.method: The paper analyzes how different scoring approaches affect error localization: 1) scoring operations by surprise given immediate predecessor (local scoring), 2) scoring against longer reconstruction of intended analysis. It quantifies error spread, develops procedures for controlling false positive rates under exchangeability assumptions, and examines model imperfection effects.
AI.result: The study shows that scoring choices dramatically affect error localization: local scoring causes inherited errors to be indistinguishable from correct operations, while longer reconstruction spreads single mistakes across many operations. The paper provides statistical guarantees for false positive control and reveals that representation dimension rather than training data volume is the binding constraint for error attribution.
AI.conclusion: There exists a fundamental limit on error attribution where small errors become indistinguishable from normal variation among sound analyses. This limit decreases slowly with more training data but is primarily constrained by representation dimension, making current large representation sizes a significant limitation for reliable auditing of autonomous data analysis agents.

title: Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Published in The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
summary: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

AI.tldr: A vision-based framework for continuous workpiece localization in hot forging factories using multi-camera monitoring of handling equipment with event-driven state machines and activity recognition.
AI.motivation: Direct workpiece tracking in hot forging is unreliable due to extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing, creating need for alternative localization methods.
AI.method: Equipment-centric framework using multiple static 2D cameras to track handling equipment, estimate 3D coordinates, recognize grasp/release activities via keypoint-guided attention in 3D CNN, and validate events with finite state machines.
AI.result: Achieved 100% event detection accuracy (33-second tolerance), mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and mean system latency of 21 seconds in operational hot forging factory.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning, enabling continuous workpiece localization and supporting visualization and quantitative analysis in challenging industrial environments.

title: EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Benchmark, dataset (304 budget-conditioned agent tasks), and evaluation harness; artifacts to be released
summary: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

AI.tldr: EcoAgent-Bench introduces a new benchmark where AI agents must complete tasks within explicit budgets, measuring not just task completion but also economical resource usage across 304 real-derived tasks.
AI.motivation: Current agent benchmarks focus primarily on task completion while treating resource use as secondary. In real-world deployment, agents need to make economic decisions about when to escalate (use more expensive resources/models), when to use cheaper alternatives, and how to manage limited budgets effectively.
AI.method: Created EcoAgent-Bench with 304 real-derived tasks spanning five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue. Each task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. The benchmark tests four key decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting appropriate model tiers, and stopping on unsupported premises. Evaluated seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings with four oracle scripted controls.
AI.result: Tool-API agents achieved only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency). They often either stopped before warranted escalation or overspent on cheap tasks. Always-escalate controls achieved high micro success but failed save-oriented tasks. GPT-5.4's escalation rate changed from 0% to only 3% with threshold-crossing budget sweep.
AI.conclusion: Task completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. Current LLM agents struggle with economic decision-making, highlighting the need for benchmarks that measure both efficiency and effectiveness. The authors release all materials needed for further study of economical agent behavior.

title: Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles
summary:
The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

AI.tldr: Researchers develop a shape-constrained predictive modeling approach for nanoparticle properties that reduces experimental screening needs in nanotherapeutic development.
AI.motivation: Nanotherapeutics development requires extensive empirical optimization due to sensitivity of nanoparticle properties to minor process parameter changes, lacking predictive frameworks that increase costs and development time through iterative experimental screening.
AI.method: Using controlled microfluidic methods to prepare liposomes and lipid nanoparticles under varying conditions (lipid concentrations, flow rates, mixing ratios), then developing and validating a shape-constrained predictive model informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge.
AI.result: Shape-constrained modeling enables accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity (PDI), reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows while supporting rational and efficient nanomedicine process development.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a predictive mathematical approach for nanoparticle characteristics that enhances efficiency in nanotherapeutic development by minimizing empirical optimization requirements.

title: Hyper-ES: Effective Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning via Descent Direction Merging
summary: Evolution Strategy (ES) is a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for resource-constrained Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective. In such high-dimensional parameter spaces, most random perturbations are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. We propose Hyper-ES, a subspace-based ES framework that avoids the weakness of ES in full-parameter search while exploiting its strength in low-dimensional optimization. Instead of asking ES to discover useful directions from random perturbations in the LLM parameter space, Hyper-ES first performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions. Although each direction may provide only a limited improvement on its own, their span forms a compact adaptation subspace that captures useful reasoning updates. Hyper-ES then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than over arbitrary full-model perturbations. We evaluate Hyper-ES on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Results show that Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates. Code at https://github.com/kuangrepi/Hyper-ES.

AI.tldr: Hyper-ES is a subspace-based Evolution Strategy framework that combines gradient-based fine-tuning to find useful adaptation directions, then uses CMA-ES to optimize merging coefficients in this subspace, enabling efficient LLM reasoning improvement with fewer gradient updates.
AI.motivation: Direct application of Evolution Strategy (ES) to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective because in high-dimensional spaces, most random perturbations are orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. There's a need for efficient fine-tuning methods that work well for resource-constrained LLM reasoning.
AI.method: Hyper-ES uses a two-stage approach: 1) First performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions, whose span forms a compact adaptation subspace capturing useful reasoning updates. 2) Then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than arbitrary full-model perturbations.
AI.result: Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets, while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates.
AI.conclusion: Hyper-ES effectively combines the strengths of gradient-based fine-tuning and Evolution Strategy by operating in a learned subspace of meaningful descent directions, providing an efficient alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for LLM reasoning with better performance and reduced computational requirements.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, submitted to journal(Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing) and under review
summary: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture for laser powder bed fusion that integrates an ontology-driven reasoning system with statistical learning to control melt pool quality, successfully eliminating overhang dross defects while maintaining process constraints.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of controlling quality defects (specifically overhang dross) in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, where critical quality parameters like melt pool depth cannot be directly measured during the build process. There's a need for intelligent control systems that can handle complex geometric dependencies and ensure quality while maintaining process constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose a geometry-conditioned neuro-symbolic architecture featuring: 1) A standards-aligned ontology that operates inside the control loop, linking process objectives/constraints to observable controller signals, 2) A description-logic reasoner that converts constraints into references and bounds for each scan, 3) A Gaussian process that provides geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio with calibrated uncertainty, 4) A constraint-aware predictive controller that uses a small quadratic program per scan, 5) Feature classification to select active constraints based on geometry (adding lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, monotone guards beyond calibrated range, and energy-density caps).
AI.result: In simulations using an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture: 1) Eliminates dross produced by geometry-blind controllers, 2) Holds dross at zero with only small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, 3) Degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, 4) Retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code, demonstrating adaptability and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes architectural feasibility for neuro-symbolic control in laser powder bed fusion, showing that integrating symbolic reasoning with statistical learning can effectively control unobservable quality parameters through observable proxies. The principal next step identified is experimental calibration of the depth-to-width ratio in real manufacturing settings.

title: SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution
