summary: LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon tasks through tool use and environment interaction, shifting evaluation from final-response scoring to verification of complete executions. For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. However, existing judge benchmarks often expose final responses or static trajectories, and rarely combine task-time skills with directly inspectable artifacts and environments. We therefore introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification for both LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge methods. Additionally, we propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. On a disjoint development pool, an automated evolution loop further refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases. On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/SkillTV-Bench

AI.tldr: SkillTV-Bench: A benchmark for evaluating skill-aware trajectory verification in LLM agents, with SkillTV-Evolve that creates reusable JudgeSkills to improve agent judgment accuracy by 14.8 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing verification methods for LLM agents fail to properly account for task-time skills - procedural knowledge that indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are critical. Current judge benchmarks often only expose final responses or static trajectories without combining skills with inspectable artifacts and environments.
AI.method: 1. Created SkillTV-Bench: 681 real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across 11 domains for evaluating skill-aware trajectory verification. 2. Developed SkillTV-Evolve: externalizes verification knowledge as reusable JudgeSkills that guide agent judges to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. 3. Used automated evolution loop to refine JudgeSkills using misjudged cases from a disjoint development pool.
AI.result: The refined JudgeSkill improved the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points on SkillTV-Bench. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increased selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts.
AI.conclusion: SkillTV-Bench addresses the gap in skill-aware trajectory verification evaluation, and SkillTV-Evolve demonstrates that reusable JudgeSkills can significantly improve verification accuracy and selection of successful trajectories, making agent evaluation more reliable.

title: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

AI.tldr: GROM: A one-shot gradient-free analytical approach for machine unlearning in LLMs that's orders of magnitude faster than fine-tuning while maintaining effectiveness against quantization attacks.
AI.motivation: Current gradient-based unlearning methods are computationally expensive, lack analytical formulations, and merely hide knowledge rather than removing it (as shown by quantization attacks that restore forgotten content).
AI.method: Frames unlearning as ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving closed-form additive updates for targeted weight matrices. Uses gradient-free forward passes only, no backpropagation or iteration, applying weight edits in seconds.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP datasets, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing model performance. Withstands low-bit quantization attacks.
AI.conclusion: GROM provides an efficient, effective one-shot unlearning solution that directly removes sensitive content from weights rather than masking it, addressing key limitations of current gradient-based approaches.

title: StepReflect: Structured UI Transition Reflection for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Autonomous mobile GUI agents require accurate action reflection for reliable long-horizon execution. Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

AI.tldr: StepReflect is a supervised structured prediction approach for GUI agent reflection that outperforms zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 points in transition accuracy and reduces API costs while achieving competitive task success.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous mobile GUI agents rely on costly open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is inefficient and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions.
AI.method: Formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. Uses staged training pipeline with supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement.
AI.result: Achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld (exceeds zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points). Online evaluation shows higher task success in 3 of 4 agent configurations and reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all configurations.
AI.conclusion: StepReflect establishes a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents, offering better accuracy and cost efficiency.

title: Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts
summary: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

AI.tldr: Paper studies ex ante difficulty prediction for AI agents across diverse benchmarks, identifies limitations of AUC metrics, finds token-level entropy as useful predictor, and uses difficulty residuals to detect environment flaws.
AI.motivation: Reliably estimating task difficulty before execution would help environment designers calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula, especially important for long-horizon domains where trial-and-error is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Studied difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. Analyzed AUC limitations and identified token-level entropy as a predictive signal.
AI.result: Showed that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identified token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and demonstrated how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive study of difficulty prediction across diverse agentic domains, offering practical methods for improving evaluation benchmarks and revealing how difficulty analysis can identify underlying environment issues.

title: Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows
comment: Accepted at AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
summary: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that evaluating generative AI systems requires focusing on "epistemic warranted reliance" - conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs to their own reasoning, beyond just assessing accuracy, fairness, or explainability.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly used in high-stakes professional contexts where outputs shape user beliefs and decisions. Current evaluation frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, explainability, safety, or user trust, but don't directly address when users are epistemically justified in relying on AI outputs.
AI.method: Develops a normative framework based on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, identifying three necessary conditions: epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice. Applies this framework through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring.
AI.result: The framework identifies specific harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability fail to address, showing how failures of the three epistemic conditions can lead to consequential problems in professional contexts. The analysis demonstrates the insufficiency of evaluating AI systems solely based on output correctness.
AI.conclusion: GenAI systems should be designed and evaluated around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone, requiring attention to how systems enable proper epistemic positioning of users in relation to AI-generated information.

title: Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation
summary: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

AI.tldr: A learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient tensor-network contraction plans for quantum circuit simulation on GPUs, achieving better performance than traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is computationally expensive and its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. While tensor-network contraction can reduce costs by exploiting circuit structure, the efficiency depends heavily on the chosen contraction plan, with GPU performance varying significantly even among plans with similar theoretical complexity.
AI.method: Presents a learning-to-rank framework for contraction plan selection. Each plan is represented by structural features derived from its sequence of pairwise contractions. Gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives, and evaluated on diverse circuit families with in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets.
AI.result: Learned rankers generally identify better plans than random and MinFill-based baselines, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. Models retain useful decision quality when tested on different GPU architectures without retraining, though performance remains partly backend dependent.
AI.conclusion: Learning to Rank is a practical approach for reducing contraction-plan search overhead while maintaining performance, though backend dependence remains a factor to consider. The framework demonstrates substantial cross-architecture stability while acknowledging partial backend dependency.

title: Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy
summary: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

AI.tldr: Large language models often reverse their initial stance to align with user preferences (preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy), and this can be automatically detected from single responses using a novel framework called CAP that collects labeled data across multiple models.
AI.motivation: Sycophantic responses are pervasive in LLMs and can be harmful. The paper focuses on a specific harmful type called preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where models reverse their initial stance to align with user preferences. Existing research mainly measures sycophancy levels, but this work asks whether PSRS can be automatically detected from single responses.
AI.method: Introduces CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applied CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, collecting 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. Investigates three research questions: frequency of PSRS occurrence, detection feasibility, and cross-model generalization of detection.
AI.result: PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Detection of PSRS from response text alone is feasible, but detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from training data. Detection performance drops on unseen models, highlighting cross-model generalization challenges.
AI.conclusion: PSRS is a measurable problem in LLMs, automatic detection is possible but faces cross-model generalization challenges. The paper provides a dataset and framework (CAP) for future research on detecting harmful sycophantic behaviors in language models.

title: Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention
summary: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

AI.tldr: FERL is an interpretable classification method that learns fuzzy rule models with evidential outputs, providing direct belief measures, plausibility scores, and abstention capabilities without post-hoc calibration.
AI.motivation: Real-life interpretable classification needs more than just accurate predictions - models should be transparent about decision evidence and have reliable abstention mechanisms when uncertain.
AI.method: Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL) learns interpretable fuzzy rule models whose evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) arise directly from fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, without auxiliary heads, held-out sets, or repeated inference.
AI.result: FERL achieves statistically significantly higher accuracy (+2.6% average) across 30 tabular datasets, best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers, high set coverage (0.92 vs. ≤0.82), matches dedicated OOD detectors (77.7 vs. 77.4 AUROC), and performs well on concept-bottleneck evaluations.
AI.conclusion: FERL provides a unified framework for interpretable classification with built-in evidential reasoning, combining high accuracy, transparency, uncertainty quantification, and OOD detection while maintaining theoretical properties like Lipschitz stability.

title: SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation
summary: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

AI.tldr: SkillHEX: A framework for autonomous LLM skill evolution using hypothesis-driven self-verification and evidence-guided tree search to overcome sparse rewards and exploitation traps in real-world deployments.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM agent deployments require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, but face challenges: limited interaction budgets, lack of training/validation sets, sparse rewards, and outcomes that conflate multiple latent failure causes. Existing methods that greedily refine single skills are vulnerable to exploitation traps where early misdiagnoses exhaust limited trials.
AI.method: SkillHEX couples hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. It translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests that produce diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides search over persistent skill-revision branches, balancing exploitation of supported edits with exploration of plausible alternatives.
AI.result: Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods, achieving average pass rates of 55.9% (GPT-5.3-Codex) and 57.9% (Claude Opus 4.7) under five-iteration budget constraints.
AI.conclusion: SkillHEX provides an effective closed-loop framework for autonomous skill evolution in resource-constrained real-world settings, overcoming the sparse reward challenge and exploitation traps that plague existing approaches through systematic hypothesis testing and evidence-guided exploration.

title: Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation
comment: 6 pages. Accepted in 36th Irish Signals and Systems Conference (ISSC) 2026
summary: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

AI.tldr: Comparative evaluation of three post-hoc analysis methods (Random Forest, LIME, PCA) for pattern detection in clustering results using synthetic datasets with injected patterns.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental challenge in interpreting clustering outcomes, especially in domains like healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. Existing explainability techniques are designed for feature importance or local instance-level explanations, not for identifying structured patterns within clusters.
AI.method: The paper introduces synthetic datasets with systematically injected predefined patterns to enable controlled evaluation. It compares three widely used techniques: Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis.
AI.result: Results show that while each method can recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. This reveals a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for dedicated pattern detection methodologies specifically designed for cluster interpretation, as current post-hoc analysis methods are insufficient for comprehensive pattern detection in clustering results.

title: Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) Model: A Computational Account of What Makes Design Options Worth Trying
summary:
This paper proposes the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, which formalizes the value of trying a candidate design action as its expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action--outcome relations. The model addresses one part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question concerning how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection. We examine two environmental properties: generalizability, or how far knowledge from one trial extends to neighboring candidates, and outcome discriminability, or how clearly differences among outcomes can be distinguished.
  We tested the model through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action--outcome relations under a limited trial budget. Epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability in the simulations. In the human experiments, the subjective value of trying and enjoyment followed inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflected both properties.
  The B-EUR model provides a computational account of candidate-action evaluation within uncertainty-driven design activity and offers implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

AI.tldr: B-EUR model formalizes candidate design action value as expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action-outcome relations, tested via simulations and human experiments showing inverted-U relationship with generalizability and increased value with outcome discriminability.
AI.motivation: To address part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question about how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection, and to understand how environmental properties like generalizability and outcome discriminability affect uncertainty-driven design activity.
AI.method: Proposed Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model that quantifies value of trying candidate designs based on expected epistemic uncertainty reduction. Tested through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action-outcome relations under limited trial budgets.
AI.result: Simulations showed epistemic value follows inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increases with outcome discriminability. Human experiments showed subjective value of trying and enjoyment follow inverted-U relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflects both properties.
AI.conclusion: B-EUR provides computational account of candidate-action evaluation in uncertainty-driven design, with implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

title: Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: FALM-PINN is a new optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting using Fourier-enhanced basis and alternating Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, achieving significantly better accuracy on high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs often fail on PDEs with high-frequency/multi-scale solutions and strongly nonlinear problems due to spectral bias (neural networks underfitting high frequencies) and representation-coefficient coupling (entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting in a single nonconvex optimization).
AI.method: Proposes FALM-PINN with alternating optimization: upper-level learns Fourier-enhanced basis to enrich latent space with high-frequency components; lower-level fits projection coefficients on this basis using Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. For linear PDEs, reduces to single-step convex optimization.
AI.result: Achieves relative L² errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs. Proves global convergence of the alternating training scheme for both linear and nonlinear PDE cases.
AI.conclusion: FALM-PINN successfully addresses key limitations of standard PINNs by decoupling representation learning from coefficient fitting, enabling accurate resolution of high-frequency and strongly nonlinear PDE problems with proven convergence guarantees.

title: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

AI.tldr: A verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework improves LLM reasoning by using test-time compute to both explore multiple reasoning trajectories and refine each through self-critique before majority voting aggregation.
AI.motivation: Current test-time scaling approaches have limitations: wider sampling alone suffers from diminishing returns due to repeated answer patterns, while verifier-based selection depends heavily on external reward model calibration. There's a need for more effective ways to utilize test-time compute for reasoning improvement.
AI.method: Proposes a breadth-depth refinement framework that: 1) Samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts (breadth), 2) Refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction (depth), 3) Aggregates refined answers via majority voting. This combines exploration of diverse attempts with local error repair.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms baseline methods (greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, lookahead decoding) across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500 datasets. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, improved MATH500 accuracy from strongest verifier baseline to 58.0% and AMC from 25.0% to 32.5%.
AI.conclusion: Test-time compute is more effective when used to refine sampled reasoning trajectories rather than only sampling more candidates or relying on verifier-guided selection. The breadth-depth framework provides verifier-free improvement by balancing exploration diversity with local error correction.

title: CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal
summary: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

AI.tldr: CohortHijack: A robustness audit showing how single-cell annotation refinement can be manipulated by removing non-target cells from the query cohort without changing the target cell itself.
AI.motivation: Many single-cell annotation tools refine initial cell labels using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. The paper investigates whether this refinement process can be manipulated while preserving the target cell's expression profile and prediction.
AI.method: Introduces CohortHijack audit that removes selected non-target cells from query cohort while keeping target expression, base prediction, and trained model unchanged. Evaluates random vs. structured removal with greedy, multi-start, and beam search on PBMC3K and Paul15 datasets using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Also tests CellTypist majority voting.
AI.result: Structured removal consistently outperformed random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing small fractions of cohort. Effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement disabled. CellTypist majority voting also vulnerable - refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals.
AI.conclusion: Query cohort composition serves as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation, revealing vulnerabilities in refinement-based annotation tools.

title: A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition
summary: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

AI.tldr: INTraJ is a trajectory prediction framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: planning (using future social info) and reaction (making local adjustments), improving prediction stability and accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory prediction methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence. The authors observe that agents typically form motion plans by first anticipating others' future behaviors (planning) before making local reactive adjustments (reaction), suggesting social interactions play staged roles.
AI.method: INTraJ decomposes social influence into two stages: 1) Planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, 2) Reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. The framework supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks (Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD) demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency. State-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings.
AI.conclusion: INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The approach successfully distinguishes between planning and reactive components of social influence.

title: BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, and 13 supplementary tables (Tables S1-S13); includes Supplementary Information with detailed training and evaluation protocols. Numerical source data for all figures are provided as ancillary files; training code and the BioM-JEPA checkpoint will be released via GitHub
summary: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

AI.tldr: BioM-JEPA is a joint-embedding predictive architecture for single-cell transcriptomics that predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks instead of individual genes, improving representation quality and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programs, but most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes rather than capturing coordinated biological units.
AI.method: BioM-JEPA uses a joint-embedding predictive architecture where a student network predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks (defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence) from remaining genes, while a slowly updated teacher supplies targets from full observed gene set.
AI.result: Block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth than controls. Embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighborhood information with lowest aggregate perturbation-response error. Provided 5.75× higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76× higher embedding throughput than scFoundation.
AI.conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks are useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, offering improved biological relevance and computational efficiency.

title: Grounded Well-Condition Anomaly Detection on the Volve Field: Constructed Labels, a Baseline, and a Dual-Head Model
summary: Most public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring come from test rigs, where faults are induced on purpose and every event is known. Real production fields rarely offer that. They give you sensor histories with no fault log attached, which is exactly the situation where an anomaly-detection method has to invent its own labels, and where quiet assumptions can slip in unnoticed. We work with the open Volve field data released by Equinor and take two things seriously that such datasets usually skip. First, we build anomaly labels that are not just patterns in the numbers but are checked against what the field's own engineering documents say can physically go wrong, and we release the reasoning behind every label. Second, we test whether those constructed labels are learnable at all, using both an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head model that marks when an event happens and what kind it is, an idea we carry over from earlier work on defect detection in metal parts. The results are honest. An unsupervised detector that never sees the labels still lands on the same regions our rules flagged, which tells us the labels are not arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and event type well across wells it has never seen, and locates events in time only roughly. We report what worked, what did not, and every assumption in between. The dataset, grounded labels, per-label provenance, baseline scores, trained model, and code are released publicly under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a grounded anomaly detection approach for industrial monitoring using Volve field data, where labels are physically validated against engineering documents rather than just patterns, and tests both unsupervised and supervised models.
AI.motivation: Most public machine-condition monitoring benchmarks come from test rigs with induced faults and known events, but real production fields provide sensor data without fault logs, requiring anomaly detection methods to invent their own labels, which can lead to unnoticed assumptions.
AI.method: The authors work with Volve field data and build anomaly labels checked against engineering documents to ensure physical validity. They test label learnability using an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head supervised model that marks event presence and type, adapted from defect detection work on metal parts.
AI.result: The unsupervised detector identifies the same regions flagged by their physically-grounded labels, confirming labels aren't arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and type well across unseen wells, with rough temporal event localization. They report successes, failures, and all assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a physically-grounded framework for anomaly detection in real production fields where fault logs are unavailable. By validating labels against engineering knowledge and testing learnability, they offer a transparent, reproducible methodology. The dataset, labels, provenance, baselines, model, and code are publicly released.

title: How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?
summary: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

AI.tldr: Heterogeneous text embedding models are not universally related by simple linear transformations; compatibility depends on multiple model factors including architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution.
AI.motivation: To understand if simple transformations can translate representations across independently trained text embedding models, enabling AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text, and to test the hypothesis of latent universality in realistic text settings.
AI.method: Test lightweight translators (linear mappings) across nine heterogeneous embedding models with different architectures, pooling strategies, and training objectives. Evaluate compatibility using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), downstream transfer tasks, fidelity metrics, and retrieval performance.
AI.result: Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible model pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in literature; successful translation requires consideration of multiple model-specific factors rather than assuming universal latent relationships.

title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

AI.tldr: DreamGuard is a proactive safety guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to predict and prevent long-horizon risks, outperforming reactive approaches while maintaining low latency.
AI.motivation: Current safety guardrails for LLM agents are mostly reactive, checking only immediate actions without considering how risk evolves across the trajectory. This creates a blind spot for long-horizon risks where individually benign actions can gradually lead to hazardous states.
AI.method: DreamGuard uses a risk-aware world model that maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the agent's trajectory. It predicts future latent states and derives both immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence, then fuses these multi-horizon signals to make intervention decisions before execution.
AI.result: DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines across four benchmarks and online evaluation. It achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails and maintains an average end-to-end latency of only 25 ms per call.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that proactive guardrails using risk-aware world models are effective for preventing both immediate and long-horizon risks in LLM agent deployments, offering better safety-utility balance than reactive approaches while maintaining practical efficiency.

title: THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction
summary: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

AI.tldr: THBKG: A temporal biomedical knowledge graph that tracks evidence changes over time to predict Phase II clinical trial success by reconstructing evidence profiles as they existed at decision points, outperforming direct-evidence models.
AI.motivation: 40-50% of Phase II efficacy failures are due to inadequate target-disease linkage. Existing biomedical knowledge graphs don't allow reconstruction of evidence profiles as they existed at past decision points, making it difficult to predict which therapeutic programs will advance based on the evidence available when decisions were made.
AI.method: Created Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG) with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed. Used graph propagation on THBKG with decision-aligned benchmark to predict whether target-disease pairs entering Phase II would advance to Phase III, using only evidence available before the decision point. Adapted path-based explainer for decision-time subgraphs.
AI.result: Graph propagation over THBKG outperformed all direct-evidence reference models under the same decision-aligned protocol, achieving relative success of 4.3-4.5 at top ten pairs per therapeutic area. For the 72.8% of pairs with no direct target-disease evidence at decision points, the encoders still ranked 5-6 fold above chance by propagating through intervening biological relationships.
AI.conclusion: THBKG enables retrospective validation of therapeutic target hypotheses by reconstructing evidence landscapes as they existed historically, providing explainable predictions and improving Phase II success prediction beyond direct-evidence models, especially for cases lacking direct evidence connections.

title: Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives
summary: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes. The system then responds with feedback or a decision outcome, thereby creating a human-AI interaction loop. This thesis studies how to design and shape such interactions to achieve three goals: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy. To address these goals, the thesis is organized into three complementary parts that examine and study human-AI interactions from the perspectives of both evaluated individuals and AI systems. Together, the work presented in this thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Methodologically, this thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: This thesis develops principles and methods for designing human-AI interaction loops that help users form accurate beliefs about AI systems, encourage productive behaviors over gaming, and maintain system performance.
AI.motivation: When AI systems are deployed, users form beliefs about how they work and strategically adapt their behavior, creating human-AI interaction loops. The thesis aims to design these interactions to help users understand systems accurately, encourage productive behaviors over gaming, and ensure AI systems maintain their intended objectives like accuracy.
AI.method: The thesis integrates multiple approaches: theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations using both real-world and semi-synthetic datasets. It's organized into three complementary parts examining human-AI interactions from both user and system perspectives.
AI.result: The work advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities, addressing how to shape interactions to achieve the three stated goals.
AI.conclusion: This thesis contributes to the design of human-AI interaction loops that balance user needs with system objectives, promoting accurate user understanding while maintaining system effectiveness and discouraging harmful gaming behaviors.

title: Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control
summary: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

AI.tldr: OG-SPR combines both latent self-prediction and observation prediction to learn better visual representations for RL, using lightweight adapters to prevent over-constraining shared representations.
AI.motivation: Existing visual RL methods using either latent self-prediction or observation prediction alone struggle with sample efficiency on challenging tasks. Each approach has limitations: latent self-prediction may learn representations not grounded in observation dynamics, while observation prediction doesn't directly regularize long-term temporal predictability of latent representations.
AI.method: OG-SPR learns dynamics-aware representations through two auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. It introduces lightweight adapters for the self-prediction task to prevent over-constraining the shared representation, allowing it to benefit from predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective.
AI.result: Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from DeepMind Control Suite show OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly strong gains in challenging domains like dog and humanoid tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining both latent self-prediction and observation prediction with lightweight adapters produces more effective representations for sample-efficient visual RL, overcoming limitations of using either approach alone.

title: RA-CAD: Learning Post-Execution Critique for State-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation
summary: Text-to-CAD generation translates natural-language design intent into editable and executable parametric computer-aided design (CAD) codes, reducing the expertise and effort required for manual modeling. Existing methods incorporate fixed, externally supplied, prompt-induced, or separately optimized critique mechanisms to optimize the generation process, but they do not necessarily optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions throughout the generation process. To bridge this feedback-utilization gap, we present RA-CAD (ReAct Agent for CAD), a state-aware agent that interacts with the CAD environment through a Generate--Execute--Critique--Rewrite loop. At each iteration, RA-CAD executes the current code and observes its outcome. Conditioned on the design instruction, current code, and execution feedback, the agent then generates an explicit post-execution critique as an intermediate policy action. This critique either validates the current result for termination or provides revision-oriented guidance that conditions the next rewrite. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) first establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) subsequently applies trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization to both policy-generated code and critique sequences, assigning terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards to the complete interaction trajectory. This formulation makes critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output. Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD show that RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared with existing methods and strong proprietary language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed state-aware text-to-CAD agent.

AI.tldr: RA-CAD is a state-aware agent that uses a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop for text-to-CAD generation, with learnable critique mechanisms and optimization through CAD Code Bootstrapping and Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods have fixed or externally supplied critique mechanisms that don't optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions during generation, creating a feedback-utilization gap.
AI.method: RA-CAD operates through a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop where the agent interacts with CAD environment, executes code, observes outcomes, and generates explicit critiques that guide revisions. It uses two-phase training: CAD Code Bootstrapping (supervised fine-tuning) and Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization with F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards).
AI.result: RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks, outperforming existing methods and strong proprietary language models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed state-aware agent with learnable critique mechanisms effectively bridges the feedback-utilization gap in text-to-CAD generation, demonstrating the value of making critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output.

title: A Unified Risk View of Uncertainty: Posterior Risk for Disentanglement and Evaluation Beyond Proxies
summary: Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical in safety-sensitive applications, where understanding the sources of predictive uncertainty is essential. This often requires disentangling epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty, yet these uncertainty types are not defined consistently across the literature, making it difficult to assess whether a method produces accurate uncertainty estimates. Evaluation is further complicated by the fact that ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is typically unavailable. Existing benchmarks therefore mostly rely on proxy tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets and offer limited insight into the structure and quality of uncertainty estimates. We propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data. This view combines Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean, capturing effects such as misspecification and optimization error. This formulation constitutes the foundation of a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes. By avoiding proxy evaluations, the benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates. Empirically, we find that accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

AI.tldr: A theory-backed benchmark for evaluating uncertainty estimation methods using unified definitions of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty with semi-synthetic datasets, revealing that accurate prediction doesn't guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement.
AI.motivation: Current uncertainty evaluation lacks consistency in definitions and relies on proxy tasks (like out-of-distribution detection) that don't provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets, making it difficult to assess whether methods produce accurate uncertainty estimates, especially in safety-critical applications.
AI.method: Proposes a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk (expected loss under plausible ground-truth functions distribution), combining Bayesian uncertainty with estimator-dependent deviations. Uses semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes to enable direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.result: The benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates, revealing that accurate prediction doesn't guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. Identifies practically useful differences between methods, showing some approaches have meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark provides a theory-backed framework for direct evaluation of uncertainty estimation methods, moving beyond proxy tasks to enable comprehensive assessment of uncertainty quality and structure, with important implications for safety-critical applications.

title: BlockPython: A Process-Aware Agent-Supported Platform for the Transition from Block-Based to Python Programming
summary: The transition from block-based to text-based programming requires learners to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, which may create a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax. To support this transition, we designed and implemented BlockPython. The platform centers on bidirectional translation between blocks and Python and guides learners through four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Across these stages, learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code. During learning, the platform continuously collects process evidence, including block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, use of support, and dialogue. Deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and the learning assistant use this evidence to identify different difficulties in computational understanding and Python expression. The rule-based system is responsible for program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions. This report describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython and provides a system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and for analyzing learning processes.

AI.tldr: BlockPython is a platform designed to bridge the cognitive gap between block-based and text-based programming by providing bidirectional translation between blocks and Python, with four progressive learning stages and process-aware support mechanisms.
AI.motivation: The transition from block-based to text-based programming creates a cognitive gap for learners who must convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, making it difficult to connect computational concepts with Python syntax.
AI.method: Designed and implemented BlockPython platform with bidirectional translation between blocks and Python, featuring four learning stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. The system uses deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and a learning assistant that collects process evidence (block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, support usage, and dialogue) to identify learning difficulties.
AI.result: The platform successfully bridges the gap between program structure understanding and textual code expression by progressively establishing connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code through the four-stage learning workflow.
AI.conclusion: BlockPython provides an effective system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and analyzing learning processes, with its process-aware support mechanisms offering valuable insights into computational understanding and Python expression difficulties.

title: Do Tabular Foundation Models Agree with Themselves?
summary:
Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are currently the best approach to tabular prediction problems. They are constructed as transformers that approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution based on a pre-training prior. These univariate predictors can be converted into multivariate ones autoregressively by sampling one target and adding it to the features.
  However, the faithfulness of the resulting joint has not been investigated. Furthermore, TFMs cannot be evaluated against the posterior itself, at least not on real-world datasets, because the ground-truth distribution is unknown. We therefore propose asking a different question: could a model's predictions result from any joint distribution? To answer this question, we pose two requirements that any such model must satisfy. The first is marginalization consistency, which demands that marginalized conditionals are equal to directly predicted marginals. The second is factorization consistency, which demands that different factorization orders result in equal joint distributions. Every TFM that we evaluate violates both of these requirements for both classification and regression across all datasets.

AI.tldr: Tabular Foundation Models violate fundamental consistency requirements - their predictions cannot result from any valid joint distribution, questioning their reliability for multivariate predictions.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates the faithfulness of Tabular Foundation Models' multivariate predictions. While TFMs are currently the best approach for tabular prediction by approximating Bayesian posterior predictive distributions, their ability to produce valid joint distributions when extended to multivariate predictions via autoregressive sampling hasn't been properly evaluated. Additionally, TFMs can't be directly evaluated against true posterior distributions in real-world settings because ground-truth distributions are unknown.
AI.method: The authors propose a different evaluation approach: instead of comparing to unknown true distributions, they ask whether a model's predictions could result from any valid joint distribution. They establish two fundamental consistency requirements: 1) Marginalization consistency - marginalized conditionals must equal directly predicted marginals, and 2) Factorization consistency - different factorization orders must yield equal joint distributions. They evaluate TFMs against these requirements across both classification and regression tasks on various datasets.
AI.result: Every Tabular Foundation Model evaluated violates both marginalization consistency and factorization consistency requirements across all datasets for both classification and regression tasks. This means the models' predictions cannot be derived from any valid joint distribution, raising serious questions about their reliability for multivariate prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current Tabular Foundation Models fail fundamental consistency tests, indicating their multivariate predictions are not faithful representations of joint distributions.
