It synthesizes the literature across traditional ML, deep learning, foundation models, LLMs, and multimodal LLMs, distinguishing commonly conflated terms and mapping relationships among techniques through inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks.
AI.result: The survey produces a unified vocabulary and classification system that can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis of post-training adaptations. The taxonomy shows how adaptation strategies have evolved across different model paradigms and reveals relationships among techniques.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a framework for organizing the fragmented field of post-training adaptation. The paper concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows that require further research.

title: ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation
summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used non-invasive tools for diagnosing cardiovascular disease, but transforming multi-lead ECG recordings into reliable clinical reports remains challenging. Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Unlike image-based report-generation tasks, ECG interpretation requires the analysis of subtle temporal morphologies, followed by coherent diagnostic reasoning expressed in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems predominantly focus on classification, while current report-generation methods often produce outputs that remain inadequate for practical clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework that jointly integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder. We further introduce an ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy that helps the model focus on clinically meaningful findings. Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports. In-domain experiments on PTB-XL and cross-domain evaluation on MIMIC-IV-ECG show that ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with absolute gains of 4.0%, 6.3%, and 11.5% in METEOR, ROUGE-L, and F1-ECGBERT, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

AI.tldr: ECG-LENS: An end-to-end framework for automated ECG report generation that combines multi-lead signal modeling with clinically grounded text generation, outperforming existing methods on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Current methods produce outputs inadequate for practical clinical use as they mainly focus on classification rather than comprehensive report generation.
AI.method: ECG-LENS integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. It uses lead-wise encoders for localized waveform morphology and a global encoder for inter-lead dependencies, fuses signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts to condition a GPT-2 decoder, and employs ECG-specific report preprocessing.
AI.result: ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on PTB-XL and MIMIC-IV-ECG datasets, with absolute gains of 4.0% in METEOR, 6.3% in ROUGE-L, and 11.5% in F1-ECGBERT (a proposed ECG-specific evaluation metric) over the strongest baselines.
AI.conclusion: ECG-LENS represents a significant advancement in automated ECG report generation by effectively integrating signal analysis with clinical reasoning, addressing the limitations of existing methods and demonstrating superior performance through both standard metrics and a novel ECG-specific evaluation approach.

title: MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction
comment: 60 pages, 3 figures, 16 tables; includes Supplementary Information
summary: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

AI.tldr: MetaboLLM is a specialized language model for metabolomics that organizes heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into interpretable metabolite graphs for clinical prediction, outperforming conventional models in multiple medical applications.
AI.motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is fragmented across different resources and difficult to translate into useful predictive representations for clinical applications, creating a need for better integration and translation tools.
AI.method: Developed MetaboLLM through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval on metabolomics data. Created MetaboLLM-GIN which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using graph isomorphism networks.
AI.result: MetaboLLM outperformed base models and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge tasks. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), beating conventional models and alternative approaches. Models also produced biologically meaningful interpretations.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized language models can effectively organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations, showing promise for clinical applications.

title: GSBF: Gaussian Splatting for Environment-Aware Beamforming
summary: Beamforming plays a key role in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems. However, conventional beamforming design normally requires accurate instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and iterative optimization, which incur substantial pilot overhead and computational complexity. Recognizing that radio propagation is intrinsically governed by the physical geometry, we develop a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline based on multi-modal data, which characterizes the environment through a persistent 3D Gaussian representation. Specifically, GSBF models the environmental scattering response with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels and performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map. The rendered map is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to the constant-modulus beamformers, thereby synthesizing beams directly from the access point (AP) pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI. Simulations demonstrate that GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency.

AI.tldr: A 3D Gaussian splatting approach for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) that synthesizes MIMO beams directly from access point pose and user positions using persistent environmental representations, eliminating the need for instantaneous CSI acquisition and iterative optimization.
AI.motivation: Conventional beamforming requires accurate instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization, which leads to high pilot overhead and computational complexity. Radio propagation is intrinsically governed by physical geometry, so there's a need for more efficient, environment-aware approaches.
AI.method: Developed a GSBF pipeline using multi-modal data to create persistent 3D Gaussian representations of the environment. Uses bidirectional spherical Gaussian kernels to model environmental scattering response, performs electromagnetic rasterization to render angular propagator maps, aggregates through array-manifold dictionary, and projects to constant-modulus beamformers.
AI.result: GSBF consistently outperforms baselines like exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency, demonstrating the effectiveness of synthesizing beams directly from AP pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI.
AI.conclusion: The GSBF approach provides an efficient solution to MIMO beamforming challenges by leveraging persistent 3D environmental representations, reducing both pilot overhead and computational complexity while maintaining competitive performance compared to conventional methods.

title: RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction
summary: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall. Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

AI.tldr: Self-supervised contrastive learning framework (RxnCLF) using condensed reaction graphs achieves state-of-the-art yield prediction by learning transformation-aware reaction representations from large unlabeled data.
AI.motivation: Reaction yield prediction is limited by scarce labeled data and poor generalization of existing representations (string/fingerprint/graph-based) that only partially capture chemical transformations, especially for complex substrates.
AI.method: Propose RxnCLF - a self-supervised contrastive framework using condensed reaction graphs (CRG) that unify reactant/product information into single graphs. Pretrained on 1.7M Pistachio reactions to learn transformation-aware representations capturing reaction-center features and side chain contexts.
AI.result: RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines on multiple yield prediction benchmarks (Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, HTE C-N coupling, amide formation), improving R2 and achieving best overall performance.
AI.conclusion: CRG-based RxnCLF shows promise as a scalable reaction foundation model that can generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream tasks like regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
summary: Student mobility programs such as Erasmus+ enable students to take courses at other universities, broadening their academic and cultural horizons. However, this flexibility also leads to a practical challenge: ensuring that students do not take courses elsewhere that substantially overlap with courses in their home curriculum. In this work, we propose CourseGraph, a methodology that automates the evaluation of external courses based on insights obtained from the process followed by curriculum administrators when assessing courses for inclusion in a degree program. Course- Graph extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from the course webpage. Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

AI.tldr: CourseGraph is an automated system using BERT embeddings and Random Forest classification to identify overlapping courses between home universities and foreign institutions for student mobility programs.
AI.motivation: Student mobility programs like Erasmus+ allow students to take courses abroad, but there's a practical challenge in preventing students from taking courses that substantially overlap with their home curriculum, requiring manual evaluation by administrators.
AI.method: CourseGraph extracts course information (titles, descriptions, learning outcomes) from webpages, represents them semantically using BERT-based language models to compute pairwise similarities, and uses a Random Forest classifier to determine overlap between candidate courses and home curriculum.
AI.result: The system was evaluated using two datasets: 1) Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology with known overlapping courses, and 2) six approved international programs from Lund University with administrator decisions. Results show CourseGraph effectively identifies overlapping courses.
AI.conclusion: CourseGraph provides an effective automated approach for identifying overlapping courses in student mobility programs, supporting curriculum alignment across universities and reducing manual administrative workload.

title: Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction
summary: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the trade-off between adaptive and non-adaptive statistical testing when evaluating models on finite outcome spaces, showing that while adaptation can provide quadratic query reduction, it doesn't yield exponential advantages.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the fundamental trade-offs between adaptive testing (where later tests can depend on earlier responses) and non-adaptive testing (where all tests must be fixed in advance) in statistical model evaluation, particularly when distinguishing between different distribution classes.
AI.method: The authors work in a conditional-query model on finite outcome spaces. They analyze which distribution pairs can be reliably distinguished, then compare adaptive and non-adaptive query complexities. They construct randomized non-adaptive procedures using O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) pair queries to simulate adaptive transcripts, and build matching families to establish lower bounds.
AI.result: Key results: 1) Learnability holds iff distribution classes have positive separation in pairwise conditional probabilities. 2) When separation is zero, optimal error is exactly 1/2 for any finite query budget. 3) The worst-case adaptivity gap is Θ_ε(N²) - adaptation can reduce queries by a quadratic factor but not exponentially. 4) Constructed non-adaptive procedures with O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) queries can simulate adaptive transcripts within ρ in total variation.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive testing offers quadratic query reduction over non-adaptive testing in worst-case scenarios, but despite the apparent exponential branching possibilities of interactive evaluation, it doesn't provide exponential query advantages. The separation in conditional probabilities determines fundamental learnability boundaries.

title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
summary: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Grounded in real-world trajectories and paired with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables, these tasks cover fundamental physical processes including collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation across diverse materials and conditions. We benchmark Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and the temporal stability of inferred parameters. Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing. GAUGE lays the groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating physics fidelity in both numerical simulators and generative video world models, using real-world-grounded tasks across multiple physical phenomena and materials.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of physical fidelity in simulators and video world models rely on perceptual similarity or human judgments, which provide limited insight into specific physical principles being violated.
AI.method: Creates 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects, grounded in real-world trajectories with calibrated physical metadata and uncertainty annotations. Benchmarks Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families, and evaluates 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks.
AI.result: No uniformly faithful physics engine exists, with largest discrepancies in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Video world models can produce trajectories with correct equation form but recover incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.
AI.conclusion: GAUGE establishes groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence by providing systematic evaluation of physical fidelity across diverse phenomena.

title: The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity
summary: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

AI.tldr: SG-TULA is a new subgradient-based Langevin algorithm that handles non-smooth, superlinear growth, non-convex potentials with explicit convergence bounds, validated on LLM pretraining.
AI.motivation: Current sampling methods struggle with target distributions that combine non-smoothness, superlinear gradient growth, and non-convexity simultaneously, while existing subgradient Langevin algorithms lack competitive convergence rates.
AI.method: Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA) - a discretization of Langevin diffusion using subgradients directly without smoothing, with taming techniques for stability in superlinear regimes, producing an explicit, stable scheme.
AI.result: Non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance with explicit constants in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms; excess risk estimates for optimization; competitive pretraining of GPT-2 lineage LLM against AdamW and Muon.
AI.conclusion: SG-TULA provides a theoretically sound and practical method for sampling from challenging distributions with provable guarantees, demonstrated effective for large-scale machine learning applications like LLM pretraining where existing methods lack comparable non-asymptotic analysis.

title: VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

AI.tldr: VLMs struggle to annotate video game frame sequences with reward signals due to extreme variability in synthetic scenarios and poor physics compliance, requiring techniques like output mixing and prompt optimization to improve performance.
AI.motivation: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and AI agents have revolutionized real-world applications but have limited adoption in video games due to synthetic scenarios' extreme variability and poor compliance with real-world physics. The authors investigate using VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals for applications like conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning.
AI.method: The study shows VLMs often struggle with basic questions on racing video games (and other game genres). The authors discuss countermeasures including VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. They also examine how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect annotation quality and token consumption.
AI.result: VLMs frequently struggle to answer basic questions about video game scenes, particularly in racing games. The research demonstrates that techniques like VLM output mixing and prompt optimization can help improve performance. The analysis reveals how various factors (sequence length, resolution, question batching) impact both annotation quality and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: While VLMs have potential for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, their current limitations in handling synthetic gaming environments necessitate careful optimization of prompts, output mixing strategies, and consideration of computational factors to make them practically useful for applications like conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning.

title: Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data
summary: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Surv-IPTB is a novel attention-based framework that directly estimates individual treatment benefit probabilities in survival analysis using pairwise comparisons and handles censoring through imprecise probabilities.
AI.motivation: Need for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival analysis contexts, particularly to quantify the probability that specific patients will experience extended survival under treatment versus control, going beyond conventional average treatment effect estimation.
AI.method: Reformulates IPTB estimation as binary classification using pairwise patient comparisons across treatment/control cohorts. Incorporates principled handling of right-censored observations via imprecise probability representations (interval-valued probabilities). Uses attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations for flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons while learning soft class probabilities for censored cases.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures (spiral, bell-shaped, circular feature spaces) show robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. Consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner, S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox PH, and Beran estimators, especially in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods degrade significantly.
AI.conclusion: The attention-based framework establishes a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The approach demonstrates superior performance in complex nonlinear scenarios compared to existing methods.

title: Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

AI.tldr: Using Vision Language Models to extract human-defined rewards from gameplay videos, enabling offline RL training without direct game engine access.
AI.motivation: RL requires game engine access for rewards, involves difficult reward design/tuning, and suffers from sparse rewards that make policy analysis challenging.
AI.method: Annotate video game datasets using Vision Language Models (VLMs) to extract human-defined rewards from gameplay videos, then apply offline RL to train conditioned agents.
AI.result: Successfully trained conditioned agents that respond to desired returns using VLM-extracted rewards and offline RL, though difficulties and limitations were identified in early experiments.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can facilitate reward extraction from gameplay videos, making RL more accessible by eliminating need for direct engine access and simplifying reward design, though challenges remain.

title: BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians
summary: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

AI.tldr: BaKron is an efficient quantization algorithm that combines GPTQ-style adaptive rounding with two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations, achieving cubic scaling while capturing richer curvature information.
AI.motivation: Existing GPTQ-style quantization uses only one-sided activation information, missing output coordinate correlations. Two-sided Hessian approximations capture richer curvature but are computationally expensive in the vectorized weight domain. There's a need for efficient quantization algorithms that can leverage better curvature information without prohibitive computational costs.
AI.method: BaKron builds on two-sided adaptive rounding (from BoA/YAQA) using anti-diagonal parallelism and recursive divide-and-conquer. It operates on m×n weight matrices with O(m+n) sequential steps, reducing total work from O(m²n²) to O(mn(m+n)). The algorithm is modular - compatible with different base quantizers and Hessian estimators.
AI.result: BaKron achieves cubic scaling (O(mn(m+n))) matching GPTQ while exploiting richer two-sided Hessian information. The paper provides practical benchmarks, evaluates various Hessians BaKron can use, develops efficient Hessian computation techniques, and presents experimental evaluation showing the algorithm's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: BaKron successfully bridges the gap between computational efficiency and curvature exploitation in neural network quantization, offering a modular framework that maintains GPTQ's scalability while utilizing superior two-sided Hessian information for better quantization quality.

title: Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process
summary: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

AI.tldr: Comparison of three ranking-dependent pairwise comparison methods (Best-worst, Best-Second Best, maximum difference) for Analytic Hierarchy Process to reduce expert comparisons while maintaining quality.
AI.motivation: To improve decision support by reducing the number of comparisons experts need to perform while maintaining data quality, using ordinal information to enhance expert data estimation in uncertain environments.
AI.method: Comparison of three ranking-dependent pairwise comparison patterns: Best-worst method (incomplete), Best-Second Best/Top 2 method (incomplete), and original maximum difference method (can be complete). Analysis of conditions for comparing methods in terms of stability to expert errors, supplemented by simulation-type experiments.
AI.result: Determined conditions for comparing the three methods regarding stability to expert errors, identified the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison pattern, and showed that the number of comparisons can be reduced without losing credibility of expert session results.
AI.conclusion: The research successfully identifies optimal comparison patterns that reduce expert workload while maintaining decision quality, contributing to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision
summary: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD) enables LLM self-improvement without external supervision by using internal consistency and majority voting to create pseudo-solutions, then distilling from the shortest correct completion into the longest incorrect one.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods still rely on external supervision like ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or larger model guidance, failing to achieve genuine "self"-distillation without external help.
AI.method: U-OPSD samples multiple rollouts, constructs pseudo-solutions via majority vote under self-consistency threshold, conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution, and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion.
AI.result: U-OPSD consistently improves base models across diverse benchmarks and matches/surpasses supervised methods. On AIME24-25, HMMT25, MATH500, AMC23, improves Qwen3 by 8.5-10.7% over base models and outperforms OPSD by average 2.3-3.2%. In thinking mode, matches or outperforms OPSD and surpasses GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised on-policy self-distillation using internal consistency alone is feasible and effective, enabling LLMs to self-improve without external supervision while matching or surpassing supervised methods.

title: Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment
summary: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

AI.tldr: A novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment for climate data super-resolution that captures temporal correlations between frames to improve resolution enhancement.
AI.motivation: High-resolution climate data is expensive to acquire but crucial for meteorological predictions. Current deep learning approaches focus mainly on single-frame spatial information and ignore temporal correlations between frames. Additionally, climate data is stochastic and noisy, making traditional temporal alignment methods like optical flow ineffective.
AI.method: Proposes a Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment: 1) Paired Latent Mapping for spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces, 2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment that captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames, and 3) Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution that optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR.
AI.result: Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated superior performance of the proposed framework compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively addresses the challenge of capturing implicit temporal correlations in climate data SR, overcoming limitations of traditional methods and improving super-resolution performance through bidirectional temporal alignment and latent space unification.

title: RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction
summary: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

AI.tldr: RRC enables generative reward models to effectively support reinforcement learning by converting comparative reward modeling into ranking-based rewards through self-competitive and anchor-guided ranking strategies.
AI.motivation: Generative reward models show strong capabilities in response ranking but have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning due to a mismatch between comparative reward modeling and scalar scoring paradigms used by existing RL algorithms.
AI.method: Proposes Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) with two strategies: (1) self-competitive ranking exploiting comparisons among sampled responses, and (2) anchor-guided ranking enabling scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses.
AI.result: Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks show RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches.
AI.conclusion: RRC bridges the gap between comparative generative reward modeling and RL algorithms by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings, unlocking the potential of generative reward models for reinforcement learning applications.

title: AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

AI.tldr: AgentOPSD: A critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic RL that aggregates token-level teacher-student gaps into turn-level evidence and uses Bayesian belief updates to identify pivotal turns.
AI.motivation: Standard RL with verifiable rewards fails to properly credit pivotal decisions in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. While recent privileged self-distillation provides denser supervision, it lacks clear representation of sequential credit assignment.
AI.method: AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This creates a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals, identifying pivotal turns through marginal belief revision between states.
AI.result: AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models (3B and 7B scales), achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablations show gains come from turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.
AI.conclusion: AgentOPSD provides an effective critic-free approach for turn-level credit assignment in agentic RL, requiring no additional critic or extra rollouts while being fully compatible with standard policy optimization. The method successfully addresses the sequential credit assignment problem through principled Bayesian belief updates.

title: CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks
summary: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

AI.tldr: CalibForge is an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses solver calibration to create challenging yet learnable tasks for terminal agent training.
AI.motivation: Current terminal agent training lacks appropriately challenging tasks - existing approaches only verify task feasibility but don't calibrate difficulty relative to specific solver capabilities.
AI.method: CalibForge uses adversarial solver calibration with two strategies: multi-solver calibration targeting disagreement within heterogeneous solver pools, and contrastive solver calibration targeting strong-pass/weak-fail relations between solvers.
AI.result: System generated 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Models trained on these tasks achieved 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with improvements up to 24.71-30.04 percentage points over base models across three benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data, as demonstrated by significant performance gains across multiple benchmarks.

title: OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents
summary: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

AI.tldr: OPERA: An operator-residual framework that improves autonomous optical experiments by using physically interpretable operators and residuals to guide agent decisions, reducing misleading score-only feedback and experimental budgets.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous agents in optical experiments use scores that may not reflect actual experimental success, leading to misleading feedback where scores increase without physical improvement.
AI.method: OPERA framework uses optical operators (representing executable changes to measurement, control, or reconstruction) and physically interpretable residuals (reporting departures from specified physical conditions). Agents use both to select, combine, or generate operators.
AI.result: Across three optical tasks: score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6-39.0% of decisions vs. 0.9-1.9% for operator-residual feedback. OPERA increased probability of reaching/maintaining task targets, reduced experimental budgets, and successfully transferred protocols from digital twins to three optical instruments with lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Operators and residuals together guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence, making experimental feedback more reliable and physically meaningful than score-only approaches.

title: An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a learner for agnostic PAC learning that achieves statistically optimal risk bounds matching known lower bounds, settling the sample complexity question up to universal constants.
AI.motivation: Agnostic PAC learning sample complexity has been an open problem - previous results didn't match lower bounds, especially for all values of the optimal risk L*. The paper aims to close this gap by constructing a learner that achieves the optimal statistical risk bound.
AI.method: The authors construct a learner for a class H with finite VC dimension d ≥ 1. They analyze the binary risk L and the optimal risk L*, then derive a statistical risk bound from an i.i.d. sample of size n with probability guarantees.
AI.result: The constructed learner achieves the statistically optimal risk bound: L(ĥ) ≤ L* + C(√(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n) + (d+log(1/δ))/n) with probability ≥ 1-δ, where C = 7·10⁸ is a universal constant.
AI.conclusion: This result settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed optimal risk L*, matching the known lower bounds and thus resolving the question of optimal statistical guarantees.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems
summary: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

AI.tldr: A hybrid machine learning framework using automated sensing data for herd-level cattle weight forecasting in grazing systems, with cascade gradient boosting to random forest to neural network achieving best performance (R²=0.889).
AI.motivation: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, making cattle growth forecasting challenging. There's a need for effective forecasting methods to support agricultural decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.
AI.method: Developed a hybrid ML framework using automated sensing data (2022-2024) with weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors. Evaluated four hybrid architectures (residual, stacked, cascade, ensemble assisted) and compared against ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines. Used temporal aggregation of animal-level predictions for herd-level forecasting.
AI.result: Cascade gradient boosting to random forest to neural network architecture achieved best performance: test R²=0.889, RMSE=21.319 kg, MAE=15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures showed greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Feature importance identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid ML framework effectively forecasts cattle weight at herd level, offering potential to support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions in commercial grazing systems with irregular observations.

title: HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards
summary: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

AI.tldr: HERALD is an offline audit framework that identifies citation-laundering vulnerabilities in search agents and proposes targeted repairs through ablation studies, achieving zero empirical attack success rates while maintaining answer quality.
AI.motivation: Current search-agent reward functions combine multiple objectives (answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, anti-hacking terms), which makes it hard to determine if cited evidence was actually retrieved. High scores can be achieved through manipulation rather than genuine evidence retrieval.
AI.method: HERALD uses exact same-question interventions to test systems, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization, and conducts $2^3$ ablation studies to identify minimal repairs. It tests on Qwen3-8B models across multiple datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) with strict 5M-token matched training.
AI.result: The attack $R_0$ fails against search deletion and fake IDs but succeeds with citation-laundering. The minimal repair $R[L]$ (strengthening citation of corpus passages absent from retrieved evidence) achieves zero empirical attack success rate with 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. This repair improves citation precision (2.02 points), support recall (1.46 points), reduces unsupported citations (1.69 points), and reduces laundering attackability on 2Wiki and MuSiQue, while maintaining answer quality on HotpotQA and 2Wiki.
AI.conclusion: HERALD successfully separates robust scoring from sparse learning signals and policy transfer. The targeted repair $R[L]$ provides effective defense against citation-laundering attacks without compromising natural citation behavior, demonstrating that focused interventions can harden search agents against specific vulnerabilities.

title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
summary: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a roadmap for building Economic World Models (EWMs) - generative economic simulations where heterogeneous agents interact and co-evolve with markets and institutions, creating economic dynamics from the inside. The authors propose a six-level capability ladder for EWM systems and identify gaps in current research.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to advance beyond traditional economic models by creating generative simulations that can produce realistic economic dynamics through agent interactions, serving as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and training substrates for AI agents.
AI.method: The authors develop an implementation roadmap organized into a six-level capability ladder: 1) fixed rule-based agent worlds, 2) adaptive/LLM-based agent worlds, 3) self-evolving agents, 4) evolving institutional worlds, 5) sim-to-real economic twins, and 6) alignment with real observations. They conduct a systematic literature survey across these levels to assess current progress.
AI.result: The survey reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. Most current research focuses on simpler agent-based simulations rather than comprehensive EWMs.
AI.conclusion: The paper aims to accelerate EWM development by providing an implementation blueprint. The authors identify a significant research gap in building sophisticated economic world models and release curated resources to support future work. EWMs could serve as valuable tools for both human decision-making and AI agent training when fully developed.

title: Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis
comment: Accepted as a short paper for presentation at the 21st International Conference on Computational Intelligence Methods for Bioinformatics and Biostatistics (CIBB 2026)
summary: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

AI.tldr: A dual-level relational framework for image classification combines implicit patch-based relational learning via masked autoencoders with explicit graph-based message passing on various graph topologies, achieving improved performance on skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies in data, but there's a gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling that needs to be bridged for better image classification performance.
AI.method: 1. Baseline using EfficientNetB3. 2. Patch-based strategy with convolutional masked autoencoder for implicit inter-patch relationship learning via self-supervised reconstruction. 3. Extension with explicit relational modelling by organizing learned embeddings into graph topologies (grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour). 4. Graph Attention Networks for message passing on these structures.
AI.result: On ISIC-2018: Baseline 76.17% balanced accuracy → Implicit patch-based modelling 77.12% → Full grid-structured GAT 79.27%. On ISIC-2019: Implicit approach 59.84% → Combined implicit+explicit modelling 60.67%.
AI.conclusion: Combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance for skin lesion diagnosis, demonstrating that bridging implicit representation learning with explicit structural modelling is effective for medical image classification tasks.

title: When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories
summary: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how historical traces can hijack tool-calling agents' decision-making, introduces a benchmark for evaluating history reliability, and proposes a teacher-student policy transfer method to improve robustness against polluted histories.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling agents can be misled by historical traces that remain structurally valid but are no longer authoritative for current requests, causing the model to reuse corrupted entities or interface conventions. This history pollution can hijack otherwise correct policies.
AI.method: Introduces a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views to evaluate history reliability. Proposes a teacher-student policy transfer method where an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy trains a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes.
AI.result: On Qwen3-1.7B, the proposed method achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming baselines. The approach scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The method transfers well to clean histories, unseen functions, external benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.
AI.conclusion: History reliability is a distinct tool-use bottleneck, and reliable-state policy transfer provides an effective and scalable solution for improving agent robustness against polluted historical traces.

title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
summary: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how survey-country metadata affects LLM forecasting accuracy, testing whether verified country information improves predictions while investigating if disclosing random labels as random reduces their influence.
AI.motivation: Survey-country metadata can improve LLM forecasts when informative but may misdirect forecasts when assigned randomly, creating a need to understand when such metadata is helpful vs. harmful.
AI.method: Conducted within-record audit tests across 5 fixed API models, 6 countries, and 7 development-selected targets. Used independent population anchors and recorded human answers to measure direction and consequence. Analyzed primary 72-record panel and non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel.
AI.result: Opaque and disclosed-random labels produced similar country-direction shifts (0.214). Paired attenuation was minimal (0.0003). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040, while random-label regret included zero. Disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake, though verified metadata remained useful.
AI.conclusion: Verified country metadata is useful for improving LLM forecasting accuracy, but disclosing that a label is random does not reliably reduce its influence on forecasts.

title: Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents
summary:
Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

AI.tldr: InvestLogicBench is a new benchmark for evaluating financial LLMs that focuses on personalized investment reasoning processes (P→E→R→D→O) rather than just static QA or terminal P/L, revealing that current LLMs produce polished but weakly grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for financial LLMs are inadequate - static question answering lacks agency, while terminal profit/loss evaluation cannot determine if profitable actions were grounded, profile-consistent, or just lucky. The authors argue the community may be using the wrong metrics for consequential agents.
AI.method: Created InvestLogicBench with 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors, organized as P→E→R→D→O traces (Profile → Events → Reasoning → Decision → Outcome). The benchmark includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay.
AI.result: Testing four leading LLMs revealed logical plausibility remains near 4/5 but event grounding is only 0.8-2.8/5. Return and process quality disagree, exposing polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides.
AI.conclusion: The P→E→R→D→O framework should be a data-system interface requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance serves as a stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
summary: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini.
